fields.title: The Key Teachings of Dietrich Bonhoeffer
fields.subtitle: An Ochorus companion to his life and teaching
fields.description: A concise, faithful guide to the heart of Dietrich Bonhoeffer’s teaching — the costly grace that calls a person to follow Jesus, the Sermon on the Mount lived out in a visible community, life together as God’s gift rather than our ideal, the Psalms as the prayer of Christ, and a church that exists for others. Sixteen short chapters, each ending in questions and a prayer, written by Ochorus as an independent companion to Bonhoeffer’s ministry, naming his books for the reader’s own further study.
fields.about_html:
This is a companion to Dietrich Bonhoeffer, not a book by him. Written by Ochorus, it sets out in sixteen short chapters the teaching for which the German pastor is chiefly remembered — costly grace and the call to follow Jesus, the Sermon on the Mount taken at its word, the church as Christ present among his people, the daily disciplines of life together, the Psalms as the prayer book of the Bible, and the hard questions of responsibility, guilt and suffering that he faced in the last years of his life. It tells his life plainly, and it is honest about where readers differ from him and where his words have been bent to serve causes he never spoke for.

It is important to be clear about what this book is and is not. It is an independent work of exposition, summary and appreciation. It is not published by, affiliated with, or endorsed by any publisher or estate holding rights in the writings of Dietrich Bonhoeffer or their translations. All descriptions of his teaching are the present author’s own summaries; his books, lectures and letters are named only for the reader’s further study, and readers are warmly encouraged to obtain those works from their rightful publishers. Nothing of Bonhoeffer’s own text is reproduced here — only Scripture, quoted from the Authorised (King James) Version, and Ochorus’s account of what he taught.

Bonhoeffer spent his short life asking one question: who Jesus Christ really is for us, here and now, and what it means to follow him. The right response to his witness is not to admire the man who asked it, but to ask it ourselves, with the Bible open and the cost counted.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
Then said Jesus unto his disciples, If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me. MATTHEW 16:24

Few Christians of the twentieth century are quoted more often than Dietrich Bonhoeffer, and few are quoted less carefully. His name turns up in sermons of every kind, on posters and in speeches, pressed into service by conservatives and radicals, by pacifists and by men who wanted a theology for war. Lines he wrote are trimmed into slogans; at least one saying that circulates widely under his name, about silence in the face of evil, is found nowhere in his writings at all. He has become a kind of mirror in which every generation sees what it hoped to see. The aim of this book is to set the mirror down and look through the window instead — at what the man actually taught, and at the Lord he taught about.

He was a German Lutheran pastor and theologian, a doctor of theology at twenty-one, and the head of an illegal seminary of the Confessing Church at Finkenwalde. He opposed Hitler from the first days of the regime, was drawn through his family into the conspiracy against the dictator, and was hanged at Flossenbürg on 9 April 1945, two weeks before the camp was liberated. He was thirty-nine.

Why he still matters

Bonhoeffer matters, first, because he asked the plainest question in the New Testament and would not let it be softened. Jesus said to fishermen and tax collectors, Follow me, and they got up and went. What would it mean to take that call as seriously in the twentieth century as they took it in the first? Bonhoeffer thought the churches of his day had quietly stopped asking. They had kept the doctrine of grace and dropped the call to discipleship, and the result was a Christianity that cost nothing and changed nothing. His answer, set out in the book that English readers know as The Cost of Discipleship, is still unsettling, and still needed.

He matters, second, because he thought hard about the church — not the church as an idea, but the actual gathering of forgiven sinners who must eat together, pray together, forgive one another and bear with one another day after day. The little book Life Together, written out of the common life of his seminary, has probably done more good in more ordinary congregations than anything else he wrote. It is practical, humble and searching. It will not let a Christian love his picture of the church more than the real brothers and sisters God has given him.

He matters, third, because he did not stop thinking when the questions became terrible. In prison, with his own death likely, he went on asking what faith looks like when every prop is gone. Some of his answers were unfinished, and some have been badly used. But he asked honestly.

The one thread

If there is a single thread running through everything Bonhoeffer taught, it is this: Jesus Christ is not an idea to be held but a living Lord who is present, here and now, and who calls. Grace is costly because it comes from him and calls us after him. The Sermon on the Mount is to be obeyed because he spoke it. The church is not a religious club but Christ himself existing among his people. The Psalms are his prayer before they are ours. And the question he kept asking in his cell was, in effect, who this Christ really is for us today. The chapters that follow are all variations on that theme.

Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever. HEBREWS 13:8

How this book is arranged

The second chapter tells his life. The sixteen chapters that follow each take one of his key teachings. They begin with costly grace and the call to follow, move through the Sermon on the Mount and his teaching on Christ and the church, spend some time in the daily practices of Life Together — the day together, the day alone, listening and bearing, confession, the Psalms — and end with the harder questions of his last years: the church for others, responsibility and guilt, suffering with God, and the hope that looked past the gallows. A conclusion draws the threads together, and a reader’s guide points to his own books.

Each chapter ends with application points and a prayer. Bonhoeffer would have wanted it so. He was suspicious of a knowledge of God that never became obedience; he thought the first step mattered more than the fifth argument. So read a chapter, stop at the questions, do one of them, and pray.

A note on how he is presented

Bonhoeffer’s writings, and their English translations, are still in copyright, so this book reproduces none of his words. Everything said here is Ochorus’s own summary, and his books are named throughout so that the reader may go and read him — which is the whole point. The only words quoted are those of Scripture, from the Authorised (King James) Version.

Reading him with care

This is not a book of hero-worship, and it would be a poor tribute to a man who warned so fiercely against cheap grace to offer him cheap praise. There are four things the reader should know at the outset.

First, the conspiracy. Bonhoeffer, who in the 1930s leaned strongly towards pacifism, came to support a plot that included plans to kill Hitler. Serious Christians have disagreed about whether he was right, and still do. This book does not pretend the question is simple, and it gives both sides a fair hearing in its chapter on responsibility and guilt.

Second, the prison fragments. In letters from his cell he wrote of a world come of age and of a religionless Christianity. These were unfinished thoughts, sent to a friend, never worked out. After the war some radical theologians took them up and pressed them in directions — towards a Christianity without a personal God, or without the supernatural — that the rest of his life and writing plainly contradict. The reader should know both what he wrote and how it was used.

Third, his background. Bonhoeffer was a Lutheran, and he was trained in the liberal academic theology of Berlin, though he broke with much of it. His views of baptism, of the sacraments and of the way Scripture came to be written are not those of many evangelical readers. On the great matters of Christ, the cross, grace and obedience he speaks with a clarity that crosses traditions; on others, readers will want to weigh him carefully.

Fourth, the legend. His life has been retold with more heroism than the record allows. This book keeps to what is well established, and says so where a famous story rests on a single witness.

Prove all things; hold fast that which is good. 1 THESSALONIANS 5:21

He would not have wanted it otherwise. A disciple is not above his master, and the only one worth following is Jesus Christ.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Write down, in one sentence, what you think it costs to be a Christian. Keep the sentence and read it again when you finish this book.

2. Think of a saying you have heard attributed to a famous Christian. Before you repeat it again, find out whether he or she really said it.

3. Ask yourself honestly whether your faith is more an idea you hold or a Person you follow. What would the difference look like on Monday morning?

4. Choose a regular time to read this book slowly, one chapter at a sitting, and decide now to act on at least one application point from each chapter.

5. Read Matthew 5–7 straight through this week, at one sitting, as though you had never heard it before.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus Christ, You called fishermen from their nets and a tax collector from his table, and they rose and followed You. You call still.
Forgive me for admiring those who followed You more than I have followed You myself. Forgive me for turning Your call into an idea I can discuss.
As I read of one who counted the cost, give me honesty to count my own. Show me who You are for me today, and give me grace to obey what You show.
Keep me from making heroes of Your servants. Let me look past them to You, the only Master worth following. Amen.

fields.title: The Pastor Who Went Back
fields.body_html:
Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends. JOHN 15:13

A house of music and science. Dietrich Bonhoeffer was born on 4 February 1906 in Breslau, then in Germany and now the Polish city of Wrocław, the sixth of eight children; his twin sister Sabine arrived a few minutes after him. His father, Karl Bonhoeffer, was one of the leading psychiatrists in Germany, and when he took the chair of psychiatry in Berlin the family moved to the capital. It was a large, gifted household, full of music and conversation, where clear thinking was prized and sentiment distrusted, and which belonged to the church in the way many cultured Germans did — baptised, confirmed, and not much more. His mother, Paula, who came from a family of theologians, taught the children the Bible stories herself. The First World War reached into the house in 1918, when his brother Walter died of wounds received at the front. Dietrich was twelve.

A theologian at twenty-one. As a teenager he announced that he would study theology. His brothers, who were heading for science and law, thought he was wasting himself on a tired institution. He went ahead. He studied at Tübingen and then at Berlin, where the great liberal historian Adolf von Harnack was still teaching, and where he also read, with growing excitement, the very different theology of Karl Barth, which insisted that God speaks and man must listen. In 1927, at twenty-one, he completed his doctorate with a dissertation on the church as a community of persons, Sanctorum Communio. A year as assistant pastor to the German congregation in Barcelona followed, and then a second thesis, Act and Being, which qualified him to lecture in the university. By any academic measure he was a prodigy. By his own later account he was not yet much of a Christian.

Harlem. In 1930 he went to New York for a year of study at Union Theological Seminary. He found much of the theology there thin. What moved him lay elsewhere. A fellow student, Frank Fisher, took him to the Abyssinian Baptist Church in Harlem, and Bonhoeffer worshipped there for months, taught in its Sunday school, and heard the gospel preached with a warmth and directness he had not met in the lecture hall. He also saw, at close quarters, what racism did to the people beside him in the pews. In the same year he formed a friendship with a French pacifist, Jean Lasserre, who pressed him to take the Sermon on the Mount as a word to be obeyed. Scholars warn against making that year a single dramatic conversion, but Bonhoeffer himself later described a change in this period: he had been a theologian who used the Bible, and became a Christian whom the Bible addressed.

The young lecturer. Back in Berlin he lectured at the university, was ordained, and took on a confirmation class of rough boys in a poor district of the city, moving into the neighbourhood to be near them. His lectures on creation, later published as Creation and Fall, and on Christ date from these years.

Jamming the wheel. Hitler became Chancellor on 30 January 1933. Two days later Bonhoeffer gave a radio talk on the idea of the leader, warning that a leader who makes himself an idol becomes a misleader; the broadcast was cut off before he finished, though exactly why is uncertain. That spring the state excluded people of Jewish descent from the civil service, and a pro-Nazi party in the church, the German Christians, wanted the same rule applied to its ministers. Bonhoeffer opposed it at once. In an essay on the church and the Jewish question he argued that the church owed a duty to the state’s victims, whether they were church members or not, and that a time might come when the church must not only bandage the victims under the wheel but put a spoke in the wheel itself. The essay carries some older assumptions of his tradition about Judaism that later readers rightly find troubling; but his stand was early, and it cost him.

London and the Confessing Church. In the autumn of 1933, discouraged by the weakness of the church’s resistance, he went to London as pastor of two German congregations, and there he formed a lasting friendship with George Bell, the Bishop of Chichester. In May 1934 the Confessing Church, the movement of pastors and congregations who refused the Nazified church government, adopted the Barmen Declaration, drafted chiefly by Karl Barth, confessing Jesus Christ as the one Word of God whom the church must hear and obey. Bonhoeffer stood with its most uncompromising wing. That summer, at an ecumenical conference at Fanø in Denmark, he called on the churches to speak for peace.

Finkenwalde. In 1935 the Confessing Church asked him to lead one of its seminaries for training pastors. After a short start on the Baltic coast it settled at Finkenwalde in Pomerania. It was an unusual place: young pastors living together, beginning and ending the day with worship, meditating daily on Scripture, practising confession to one another, studying, working and playing together. The authorities regarded it as illegal. In 1936 his permission to teach at the university was withdrawn, and in 1937 the Gestapo closed the seminary and arrested a number of its former students. Bonhoeffer continued the training secretly, in scattered rural parishes. Out of these years came the two books he is most read for: Discipleship, published in 1937, and Life Together, written in 1938 and published the following year.

The voyage home. In June 1939 friends arranged for him to go to America, where he might teach and be safe. Almost at once he knew he had made a mistake. He wrote to Reinhold Niebuhr that he could have no part in rebuilding Christian life in Germany after the war if he did not share its trials with his people now, and in July he sailed home, weeks before the war began.

The conspiracy. Through his brother-in-law Hans von Dohnányi, he was taken into the Abwehr, the German military intelligence service, whose leaders included men at the centre of the resistance. Officially his church contacts abroad made him useful; in fact the post kept him from military service and allowed him to carry messages from the conspirators to churchmen overseas, including Bishop Bell. He helped in an operation that brought a small group of Jews to safety in Switzerland. He was forbidden to publish, and he spent much of this time writing his Ethics, which he never finished. He was not an assassin, whatever some retellings suggest; he was a pastor who lent the conspiracy his conscience and his cover, knowing he was stepping into guilt.

Tegel. In January 1943 he became engaged to Maria von Wedemeyer. On 5 April 1943 he was arrested, with Dohnányi, on relatively minor charges. For eighteen months he was held at Tegel military prison in Berlin. There he read, wrote, prayed, befriended guards and fellow prisoners, and sent letters — some smuggled — to his family, to Maria and to his closest friend, Eberhard Bethge, who after the war published them as Letters and Papers from Prison.

Flossenbürg. After the failed attempt on Hitler’s life on 20 July 1944, the conspirators’ papers were discovered, and Bonhoeffer’s part in the plot came to light. He was moved to the Gestapo prison in Berlin, then to Buchenwald, and in April 1945 to Flossenbürg. On 8 April, a Sunday, he led a short service for his fellow prisoners in a schoolhouse at Schönberg, where they had been held on the way. That evening he was taken away. A British prisoner, Captain Payne Best, later recalled that he asked for a message to be given to Bishop Bell: that this was the end, but for him the beginning of life. Best set it down years afterwards, and it is right to hold the words as his recollection rather than a transcript. After a summary trial Bonhoeffer was hanged at dawn on 9 April 1945 with other conspirators. Dohnányi was put to death at Sachsenhausen in the same days; his brother Klaus and his brother-in-law Rüdiger Schleicher were shot in Berlin later that month. A camp doctor’s later account of his calm prayer before death is treated by historians with caution.

What he left. An Ethics in fragments, a bundle of prison letters he never meant as a book, and a handful of short works read by millions. Above all, a life in which the question he had asked in his lectures — who Jesus Christ is, and what it means to follow him — was answered by a man who could have stayed safe and went back.

Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints. PSALM 116:15
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Bonhoeffer described a change from using the Bible to being addressed by it. Which describes your own reading this month? Choose one passage and read it this week as a word spoken to you.

2. He learned some of his deepest lessons in a congregation very unlike his own. Visit, or learn from, a church of another culture or background, and listen more than you speak.

3. He stood early for people the state had marked out. Who in your own setting is being quietly pushed to the margins? What would it cost to stand with them?

4. He went home when he could have stayed safe. Is there a place of duty you have left, or are tempted to leave, because it is hard?

5. Pray for Christians imprisoned today for their faith, by name if you can find their names.

A PRAYER
Lord God, You gave Your servant a short life and a costly witness. We thank You for his faith, and we confess that we are often more drawn to his story than to his Lord.
Speak to us through Your word as You spoke to him, not as to scholars examining a text but as to servants waiting for orders.
Give us courage to stand beside those who are pushed aside, and to stay where You have placed us when it would be easier to leave.
And when our own end comes, whenever and however it comes, let us meet it as the beginning of life, through Jesus Christ our Lord, who died and rose again. Amen.

fields.title: Costly Grace
fields.body_html:
Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto treasure hid in a field; the which when a man hath found, he hideth, and for joy thereof goeth and selleth all that he hath, and buyeth that field. MATTHEW 13:44

The book that English readers first met as The Cost of Discipleship opens with a single, sharp distinction, and it is the phrase for which Bonhoeffer is best remembered: the difference between cheap grace and costly grace. He wrote it in the mid-1930s, while training young pastors for a church under pressure, and he wrote it first of all against his own church. It has lost none of its edge.

Grace sold at a discount

What is cheap grace? Bonhoeffer described it, in effect, as grace treated like goods on a market stall, sold off at clearance prices. It is forgiveness offered without repentance. It is baptism without the discipline of the church, the Lord’s Supper without confession of sin, absolution without any personal turning. It is grace as a doctrine, a general truth, a principle — God is gracious, and therefore everything is covered — rather than as the living word of a Lord who forgives and commands in the same breath. The trouble with such grace, as Bonhoeffer saw it, is that it ends up excusing the sin instead of rescuing the sinner. It lets a man go on exactly as before, comforted that his account has been settled, and never asks him to leave anything behind.

He regarded it as the mortal danger of the church in his time. That was a strong charge from a Lutheran, and he knew it. He was not attacking the Reformation doctrine of justification by faith alone; he believed it with all his heart. He was attacking what his church had made of it. Luther, he argued, had found grace by leaving the monastery and going out into the world to obey Christ there. The grace he found cost him everything. But the generations that followed had inherited the conclusion without the journey. They had learned to say that we are saved by grace and not by works, and they had taken it to mean that works did not matter much at all.

What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid. How shall we, that are dead to sin, live any longer therein? ROMANS 6:1–2

The Apostle had seen the same danger. The answer of Romans 6 is not that grace is smaller than we thought, but that grace is a death and a new life. It does not leave us where it found us.

Grace that costs

Against cheap grace Bonhoeffer set costly grace. The two are not two different gifts; they are the same gift, received in two different ways. Costly grace is the grace of Jesus Christ received as He actually gives it — as a summons as well as a pardon. It asks for the whole life, and it gives back a life worth having. It does not wink at sin; it judges it, and then it sets the sinner free. And beneath all of this lies the deepest reason of all: this grace cost God His own Son. What God bought at such a price, we cannot treat as a bargain.

Forasmuch as ye know that ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold, from your vain conversation received by tradition from your fathers; but with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot. 1 PETER 1:18–19

To describe it, Bonhoeffer turned to the Gospels themselves — to the hidden treasure and the pearl for which a merchant parts with everything, and to the fishermen who left their boats when Jesus called. The picture is of something so valuable that giving up the rest is no longer the point. Notice that in the parable the man sells everything for joy. Costly grace is not a grim transaction in which God drives a hard bargain. It is the discovery that one thing is worth more than all the rest, and the glad letting-go that follows.

Two kinds of preaching

A church, he thought, can be orthodox in every sentence and still preach cheap grace, simply by never letting the grace it offers touch the lives of its hearers. It can say to the comfortable, you are forgiven, and never say, follow me. It can offer peace without ever mentioning the cross. The result is not a gentle church but a dead one — a people who have been assured of their salvation so often that they no longer notice they are not following anyone.

They have healed also the hurt of the daughter of my people slightly, saying, Peace, peace; when there is no peace. JEREMIAH 6:14

Jeremiah’s false prophets used the language of the covenant, but applied it where it did not belong. Bonhoeffer thought the church of his day was doing the same, and paying for it: when the state demanded its obedience, too many Christians had no habit of costly obedience to Christ with which to refuse.

A fair question

Readers from the evangelical tradition have sometimes asked whether Bonhoeffer blurred the line between grace and works — whether costly grace smuggles obedience back into the ground of our acceptance. It is a fair question, and he anticipated it. He never taught that we earn our salvation by following. He taught that the grace which saves us is the grace of a Lord who calls us, and that faith and obedience cannot be pulled apart without destroying both. Grace is free, but it is not cheap: it costs us nothing to receive and everything to keep company with. That is not far from what the Reformers themselves said, when they insisted that we are justified by faith alone, but that the faith which justifies is never alone.

For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: not of works, lest any man should boast. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them. EPHESIANS 2:8–10

Paul holds both halves in a single breath. Not of works; unto good works. Cheap grace keeps the first half and drops the second. Legalism keeps the second and drops the first. Costly grace keeps both.

There is also a pastoral caution worth adding. Bonhoeffer wrote for complacent people. A tender conscience, already crushed by its failures, may read the chapter on costly grace and hear only demand. That would be to misread him. The cost of grace was paid first by God. The call to follow comes from the one who has already carried the cross. Anyone who finds this teaching heavy should go back to where Bonhoeffer himself started: to the precious blood, and to the Lord who says, come.

Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light. MATTHEW 11:28–30

The yoke is easy. But it is still a yoke.

Counting the cost today

Every age has its own discounts on grace. The questions Bonhoeffer asked still cut. Has the grace I have received changed anything I do with my money, my time, my tongue, my ambitions? Have I heard the word of forgiveness without ever hearing the word, follow? Do I treat grace as an insurance policy or as a summons?

For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it? LUKE 14:28

Jesus told would-be disciples to count the cost before they began. He did not do so to discourage them, but to spare them the shame of a tower abandoned half-built. Bonhoeffer counted it, and paid it. The point of reading him is not to admire his account, but to settle our own.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Write down one area of your life where you have been glad of forgiveness but have never really turned. Bring it to God today, by name.

2. Read Romans 6:1–14 slowly. Mark every place where Paul says what grace does, not only what it gives.

3. If you teach or preach, look back over your last few talks. Did you offer grace without ever calling anyone to follow? Or call to follow without ever offering grace?

4. Name one concrete thing — a habit, a possession, a grudge, an ambition — that following Jesus would require you to leave behind. Take one step towards leaving it this week.

5. If your conscience is already crushed, do not start with the cost. Start with the cross. Read 1 Peter 1:18–21 each morning this week and thank God for the price He paid.

Lord Jesus Christ, You did not redeem me with silver or gold but with Your own precious blood. Forgive me for treating so costly a gift as if it were cheap.
I have been glad to be forgiven and slow to be changed. I have taken Your grace as a comfort and left it there. Call me again, and give me grace to answer.
Show me what I am holding back from You. Give me the joy of the man who found the treasure, so that selling all is no longer loss but gain.
And where my heart is already bowed down, lift it with the knowledge that You paid the price before You asked me to follow. Amen.

fields.title: The Call to Follow
fields.body_html:
And as he passed by, he saw Levi the son of Alphæus sitting at the receipt of custom, and said unto him, Follow me. And he arose and followed him. MARK 2:14

There is almost nothing in that verse. No account of what Levi was thinking, no description of his inner struggle, no explanation of what he had heard about Jesus beforehand. A man is sitting at his tax table. Jesus passes, speaks two words, and the man gets up and goes. Bonhoeffer, in the second chapter of Discipleship, made a great deal of that silence. The Gospel writer, he observed, is not interested in Levi’s psychology. He is interested in the authority of the one who calls. The only reason given for Levi’s obedience is Jesus himself.

The call, and nothing but the call

This, Bonhoeffer argued, is what discipleship is: attachment to a person. Not to a programme, not to an ideal, not to a set of rules, not even to a doctrine about Jesus, but to Jesus, who goes ahead and says, come after me. The disciple does not know where the road leads. He knows only who is walking it in front of him. That is both the terror and the freedom of it. Any Christianity that turns Jesus into a set of principles, however noble, can be admired without being followed. A living Lord cannot.

My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me. JOHN 10:27

The call also creates a break. For Levi it was the tax table; for Peter and Andrew the nets. Christ does not merely add himself to a life already full; he steps into the middle of it. Bonhoeffer went so far as to say that every other relationship — to family, to nation, to our own past — is now reached only through him, the mediator between us and everyone else.

The first step

One of the most practical things Bonhoeffer ever wrote concerns what he called the first step. Levi could not believe while sitting at the tax table. He had to get up. The step itself did not earn him anything or prove anything; but it put him in the place where faith was possible. A man who says he cannot obey until he has more faith, Bonhoeffer argued, has things the wrong way round. He must take the step that Jesus commands, and there he will find that faith is given.

From this came a pair of sentences for which Discipleship is often remembered, and which may be summarised like this: it is true that only the one who believes will obey, and it is equally true that only the one who obeys can believe. Bonhoeffer did not mean that obedience manufactures faith. He meant that the two cannot be separated, and that each is the test of the other. To the anxious Christian who takes refuge in the first half — I would obey if only I had more faith — he says the second. To the proud Christian who trusts in his obedience, he says the first.

But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves. JAMES 1:22

He added a warning that every pastor will recognise. Many a man who comes asking for help with his doubts is really avoiding a command. There is some plain thing he knows Christ wants of him, and he will not do it; and so he asks clever questions instead. The kindest answer, in such a case, is not another argument. It is to point back to the thing he has not done.

Excuses at the roadside

Luke records three men who met Jesus on the road, each of whom wanted to follow on his own terms.

And he said unto another, Follow me. But he said, Lord, suffer me first to go and bury my father. Jesus said unto him, Let the dead bury their dead: but go thou and preach the kingdom of God. LUKE 9:59–60

The word that gives them away, as Bonhoeffer noted, is first. Lord, I will follow thee; but first. Each of them set a condition, and a reasonable one. Each wanted discipleship arranged in advance. And each, in doing so, put himself in charge of the terms. Jesus will not accept that arrangement. The call does not come to us as an offer we may negotiate. It comes as a command from the one who has the right to give it.

No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God. LUKE 9:62

Single-minded obedience

The rich young man brought Jesus a question about eternal life. Bonhoeffer drew attention to the way Jesus refused to let it remain a question. The young man wanted a conversation about the good; Jesus gave him a command.

Jesus said unto him, If thou wilt be perfect, go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come and follow me. But when the young man heard that saying, he went away sorrowful: for he had great possessions. MATTHEW 19:21–22

Here Bonhoeffer introduced one of his sharpest ideas: simple, or single-minded, obedience. The church, he said, has developed a clever way of escaping the commands of Jesus. When Jesus says, sell what you have, we explain that of course he did not mean it literally; he meant that we should hold our possessions loosely, inwardly detached. And then we keep everything, reassured that our hearts are in the right place. Bonhoeffer did not deny that the inner attitude matters, nor that the command to the rich young man was a particular word to a particular man. But he insisted that the habit of interpreting every hard saying into something comfortable is itself a form of disobedience. The first question to ask of a command is not how it might be qualified, but how it might be obeyed.

Readers may reasonably ask whether Bonhoeffer himself read the Gospels too literally at points, and it is worth saying that he later recognised Discipleship carried dangers of its own; from prison he wrote that he still stood by it, while seeing its limits more clearly. But his central warning stands. There is such a thing as an interpretation that exists only to protect us from the text.

Come and die

In the chapter on discipleship and the cross comes the line for which the book is most remembered. Bonhoeffer wrote, in effect, that every call of Christ is at bottom a call to come and die. He did not mean, first of all, martyrdom. He meant the death of the old self — the letting go of our own will, our own plans, our own right to arrange our lives — which begins the moment we answer the call. For some, that death would one day be literal. He was one of them.

Then said Jesus unto his disciples, If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me. MATTHEW 16:24

Bonhoeffer was careful to distinguish the cross from ordinary misfortune. Illness, loss and disappointment come to everyone. The cross is the suffering that comes because we belong to Christ — the rejection, the loss, the shame that fall on the disciple for his Master’s sake. And he was equally careful to say that the cross is not our own invention. We do not go looking for it. It is laid on each disciple, differently, by the Lord who calls.

For whosoever will save his life shall lose it: and whosoever will lose his life for my sake shall find it. MATTHEW 16:25

That is the paradox of the call. Everything is lost, and everything is found. The disciple does not follow in order to be crushed, but to live.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Ask Jesus plainly what the next step of obedience is for you. Write down the first clear thing that comes to mind, and take that step before the week is out.

2. Notice where you say, Lord, I will — but first. Name the condition you have set, and lay it down.

3. Is there a doubt you keep raising that is really a way of avoiding a command? Be honest about it with God and with a trusted friend.

4. Choose one hard saying of Jesus you have long explained away. Before you interpret it, ask how it might actually be obeyed in your life.

5. Distinguish, in prayer, between the ordinary troubles of your life and anything you are suffering because you belong to Christ. Give thanks for the second.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You passed by and called, and men left their tables and their nets to follow You. You have called me too, and I have been slow to rise.
Forgive the conditions I have set, the reasons I have given, the clever questions I have asked to avoid a plain command.
Give me grace to take the next step, even before I see the one after it. Where I lack faith, meet me in the obedience; where I trust my obedience, humble me into faith.
I lay down my own right to arrange my life. Let me lose it for Your sake, and find it in You. Amen.

fields.title: The Sermon on the Mount
fields.body_html:
Therefore whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock. MATTHEW 7:24

For much of Christian history the Sermon on the Mount has been handled with tongs. It has been said to be meant for monks and not for ordinary believers; or for the private heart and not for public life; or for a future kingdom and not for the present age; or as a law so impossible that its only purpose is to drive us to despair and so to grace. Each of these readings contains a grain of truth. Bonhoeffer thought that together they had succeeded in doing something disastrous: they had made the words of Jesus safe. The middle and longest part of Discipleship is an exposition of Matthew 5 to 7, and its purpose is to take them out of the display case and put them back into the hands of disciples.

Spoken to disciples

Bonhoeffer began where Matthew begins.

And seeing the multitudes, he went up into a mountain: and when he was set, his disciples came unto him: And he opened his mouth, and taught them, saying. MATTHEW 5:1–2

The Sermon is addressed to people who have already been called. It is not a programme for improving society in general, nor an ethical ideal for humanity at large. It is the instruction of the Master to those who have left their nets. That is why the Beatitudes come first. They are not conditions for entering the kingdom — try to be poor in spirit, and you will be blessed — but a description of those whom Jesus has called and whom he now pronounces blessed. The poor, the mourning, the meek, the hungry, the merciful, the pure, the peacemakers, the persecuted: this is what the company of disciples looks like, and Jesus declares them happy, not because of their condition, but because of him.

Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness’ sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. MATTHEW 5:10

Salt and light

Straight after the Beatitudes comes a statement, not a command. Ye are the salt of the earth. Ye are the light of the world. Bonhoeffer stressed that Jesus does not say, try to become salt; he says, you are. The only question is whether the salt will keep its savour and whether the light will be hidden. A community of disciples is by its nature visible. It cannot follow Jesus in secret any more than a city on a hill can be hidden. It will be seen, and it will either give light or be trodden underfoot.

Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid. MATTHEW 5:14

Something more

The heart of Matthew 5, as Bonhoeffer read it, lies in a small word near its end.

And if ye salute your brethren only, what do ye more than others? do not even the publicans so? MATTHEW 5:47

What do ye more? Bonhoeffer made much of this. The righteousness Jesus requires is not merely correct; it is extraordinary. It goes beyond what decent people do anyway. Anyone can love his friends. The disciple loves his enemy. Anyone can keep the outward commandment against murder; the disciple guards his tongue against contempt. Anyone can avoid adultery; the disciple guards his eyes and his heart. Anyone can keep an oath; the disciple speaks so truthfully that he needs no oath. And the source of this extraordinary quality is not moral heroism. It is Jesus himself, who fulfils the law and who calls his disciples into his own righteousness.

For I say unto you, That except your righteousness shall exceed the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees, ye shall in no case enter into the kingdom of heaven. MATTHEW 5:20

Most searching of all, in Bonhoeffer’s treatment, are the commands about retaliation and enemies. He read Jesus as meaning what he said: that the disciple does not repay evil with evil, but absorbs it, and so brings it to an end. Evil feeds on resistance; it spends itself against one who will not strike back. And the love of enemies is not a feeling but an act — blessing, doing good, and above all praying for the one who harms us.

But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you. MATTHEW 5:44

He wrote this in Germany in the 1930s, when he had every reason to know what an enemy was. It is not the counsel of a man who had never been hurt.

The hidden righteousness

Then comes a surprise. Matthew 5 says that the disciples must be visible; Matthew 6 says that their righteousness must be hidden. Bonhoeffer saw no contradiction. The community must be seen, but its members must not do their good works in order to be seen. The extraordinary must happen, but it must not become a performance. Indeed, he said, the disciple must hide it even from himself, not keeping an eye on his own goodness, not admiring his own giving or praying or fasting. His eyes are fixed on Christ, not on his own reflection.

But when thou doest alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth: That thine alms may be in secret: and thy Father which seeth in secret himself shall reward thee openly. MATTHEW 6:3–4

This is one of the most practically useful things in all his writing. Many earnest Christians are defeated not by open sin but by the subtle pleasure of watching themselves be good. The cure is not to do less good, but to look away from it.

The narrow way

In Matthew 7, Bonhoeffer traced the life of the community among others. Disciples do not judge, because they have no standing from which to judge; they have received everything as a gift. They do not force the gospel on those who will not have it. They pray, and they trust the Father to give. And they walk the narrow way, which is narrow not because it is complicated but because it is Christ himself.

Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth the will of my Father which is in heaven. MATTHEW 7:21

The Sermon ends not with a summary but with a choice: two builders, two foundations, one storm. Hearing is not enough. The wise man hears and does.

Honest questions

Bonhoeffer’s reading of the Sermon was shaped by his friendship with the French pacifist Jean Lasserre, and in the 1930s he came close to Christian pacifism — which makes his later part in the conspiracy, discussed in a later chapter, all the more striking. But he never retracted his call to take the Sermon at its word.

Readers from the Reformed and Lutheran traditions may also ask whether this reading leaves enough room for the Sermon’s work of exposing sin and driving us to Christ. It does, provided we remember where Bonhoeffer began: these words are given to those whom Jesus has already called and blessed. The Sermon is not a ladder to climb to God. It is the path of those whom God has already come down to find, and whom he empowers to walk it.

For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure. PHILIPPIANS 2:13
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Read Matthew 5–7 in one sitting. Underline every command you have quietly decided does not apply to you.

2. Ask where your life shows something more — some love, honesty or generosity that could not be explained by ordinary decency. If you cannot find it, ask God for it.

3. Name one person who has wronged you. Pray for him or her by name, every day this week, asking good for them.

4. Do one good thing this week that no one will ever know about, and do not congratulate yourself on it.

5. Before you next give an opinion on another believer’s faults, read Matthew 7:1–5 and deal first with your own.

Lord Jesus, You sat on the mountain and taught Your disciples, and Your words have not changed. Forgive me for handling them as though they were too dangerous to touch.
Make me salt that has not lost its savour, and light that is not hidden. Give me a righteousness that goes beyond what decent people do, because it comes from You.
Teach me to bless those who curse me, to pray for those who wrong me, and to overcome evil with good.
Hide my goodness from my own eyes, and fix my eyes on You. Let me not only hear these sayings, but do them, and build my house on the rock. Amen.

fields.title: Christ the Centre
fields.body_html:
He saith unto them, But whom say ye that I am? And Simon Peter answered and said, Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God. MATTHEW 16:15–16

In the summer of 1933, while the new regime was taking hold of Germany and its universities, Bonhoeffer gave a course of lectures in Berlin on the person of Christ. He never published them. His students’ notes were gathered after his death and reconstructed, and in English they have appeared as Christology and, later, as Christ the Center. They are compressed and in places difficult. But they contain the key to everything else he wrote. For Bonhoeffer, Christian faith and Christian life begin and end with one person.

Not how, but who

Bonhoeffer opened with a question about questions. When we meet something new, he said, we usually ask how it works. We want to classify it, explain it, fit it into what we already know. Much theology has asked of Jesus Christ the same kind of question: how can God become man? How can two natures be united in one person? Bonhoeffer thought that this question, however natural, puts us in the wrong position. It makes us the masters and Christ the object of our inquiry.

The proper question is not how but who. Who are you? That is the question we ask of a person, not a thing; and when we ask it sincerely, we find that the tables have been turned. The one we are questioning is questioning us. The disciples at Caesarea Philippi did not first work out a theory of Jesus and then decide to follow him. Jesus asked them, whom say ye that I am? — and in answering, Peter found that his whole life was being claimed.

Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God. MATTHEW 16:16

Bonhoeffer pressed this point with an unexpected piece of advice: that the right way to begin speaking of Christ is with silence. He did not mean mystical wordlessness, or a refusal to preach. He meant the reverent silence of the church before the Word it did not invent and cannot master — the silence in which the creature waits to be addressed. Only out of that silence can the church speak rightly.

But the LORD is in his holy temple: let all the earth keep silence before him. HABAKKUK 2:20

Present, and for me

The second great theme of the lectures is that Christ is present. He is not merely a figure of history whose influence lives on, nor an ideal we try to imitate, but the risen Lord who is here, now, among his people. And he is present not in a vague or general way but, Bonhoeffer insisted, as the one who is for me — for us. It belongs to Christ’s very being, he argued, to be turned towards us. We cannot think of him in his majesty apart from his love for his people.

I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me: and the life which I now live in the flesh I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself for me. GALATIANS 2:20

Where is he present? Bonhoeffer answered in the terms of his Lutheran tradition: in the word preached, in the sacraments, and in the church-community. Christ is present as Word, because God speaks, and his speaking is personal address. He is present in baptism and the Lord’s Supper, because God gives himself not only to the ear but to the whole person. And he is present as the community itself, gathered in his name — a theme we shall take up in the next chapter.

For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them. MATTHEW 18:20

Evangelical readers will not all follow Bonhoeffer’s sacramental theology, and they need not. But the central claim — that Christ meets us now, and not only in memory — is one every Christian can gladly own.

The centre of everything

Bonhoeffer went on to describe Christ as the centre — of human existence, of history, and of creation. He is the centre of human existence because he stands where we have failed to stand: he is the new man before God, and our true selves are found only in him. He is the centre of history because the long hope of Israel, and the longing of every people, finds its fulfilment in him — though in a hidden way, for history does not look as if it has been conquered. And he is the centre of creation, because all things were made through him and for him, and one day all creation will be set free in him.

For by him were all things created, that are in heaven, and that are in earth, visible and invisible, whether they be thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers: all things were created by him, and for him: And he is before all things, and by him all things consist. COLOSSIANS 1:16–17

This was not an abstract claim in 1933. A regime was busy declaring that the centre of German life was the nation and its leader. To lecture that summer that Christ alone is the centre was to say something with consequences.

The humbled one

The third theme is the humility of Christ. Bonhoeffer spoke of Christ as present in the world in a kind of disguise — veiled in the form of a servant, walking among sinners, hidden in weakness. The glory of God is not displayed in him as the world expects glory, but concealed in a man who is born in a stable, rejected, crucified. Faith sees what the world does not.

For he shall grow up before him as a tender plant, and as a root out of a dry ground: he hath no form nor comeliness; and when we shall see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him. ISAIAH 53:2

This has practical consequences. A church that follows a humbled Lord must not seek power and prestige in his name, and must look for him where the world does not look — among the weak, the despised and the suffering.

And being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross. PHILIPPIANS 2:8

Honouring the creeds

A word about the ancient creeds. Bonhoeffer honoured the Council of Chalcedon, which in 451 confessed Christ as truly God and truly man in one person. He valued it chiefly for what it refused to say: it drew boundaries around the mystery rather than explaining it. That is a helpful way to read the creeds. They are not attempts to dissect Christ, but fences around a holy place, warning us off the paths that lead away from the Christ of Scripture.

And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth. JOHN 1:14

These lectures sit behind all the rest of Bonhoeffer’s work. Costly grace, the Sermon on the Mount, the church, even the strange questions from his prison cell — all circle round the same centre. The reader who wants to understand Bonhoeffer must begin where he began: not with Bonhoeffer, but with Christ.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Before your next time of Bible reading, sit in silence for five minutes. Ask not how, but who.

2. Answer Jesus’ question to Peter in your own words, in writing: Who do you say that I am? Then ask what your answer requires of you this week.

3. Read Colossians 1:15–20 slowly. List the things in your life that you have quietly treated as the centre instead of Christ.

4. Where in your community is Christ likely to be found in humility and disguise? Go there this month.

5. If you have never read one of the ancient creeds carefully, read the Nicene Creed aloud and give thanks for the fences it builds around the mystery.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus Christ, I have often asked how, and seldom asked who. I have tried to master You, when You came to be my Master.
Teach me to be silent before You, and then to speak of You truly. You are the Christ, the Son of the living God, and You are for me.
Be the centre of my life, as You are the centre of all things. Where I have put other things in Your place, dethrone them gently and take Your own.
Open my eyes to see You where the world does not look — in weakness, in the poor, in the despised — as You once came to us in the form of a servant. Amen.

fields.body_html:
For as the body is one, and hath many members, and all the members of that one body, being many, are one body: so also is Christ. 1 CORINTHIANS 12:12

Bonhoeffer’s first book was about the church. He wrote it at twenty-one, as a doctoral dissertation, and gave it a Latin title from the Apostles’ Creed: Sanctorum Communio, the communion of saints. It is a demanding book, full of the sociology and philosophy of its day, and most readers will not begin there. But the idea at its centre became one of the fixed points of his life. He summed it up in a phrase that has become famous: the church is Christ existing as community.

Not a club

Most people, if they think about the church at all, think of it as a voluntary association. People who share certain beliefs choose to meet together, as members of a society or a club might, and the church is the sum of those who have joined. Bonhoeffer did not deny that the church has a human, social shape; he spent a good part of his dissertation analysing it. But he insisted that this is not what the church most deeply is. The church is not something we create by gathering. It is something God creates, in Christ, by his Spirit, and into which we are gathered.

Now ye are the body of Christ, and members in particular. 1 CORINTHIANS 12:27

Paul does not say that the church is like a body, or that it ought to behave as one. He says, ye are the body of Christ. Bonhoeffer took that seriously. In Adam, he argued, humanity is one — one in its fall, its guilt, its isolation. In Christ, a new humanity has been created, and it too is one: one body, with Christ as its head, living by his life. The church is not a collection of saved individuals who happen to share a building. It is the new humanity already present in the world, the place where Christ is really, bodily, among his people.

For as by one man’s disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous. ROMANS 5:19

The Christ who is persecuted

There is a striking moment on the road to Damascus. Saul has been persecuting the followers of Jesus. Jesus confronts him — and says, not why persecutest thou my people, but why persecutest thou me?

And he fell to the earth, and heard a voice saying unto him, Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me? ACTS 9:4

Christ so identifies himself with his church that to strike them is to strike him. That is the heart of what Bonhoeffer meant. And it has two consequences, one comforting and one sobering. The comfort is that no believer is ever alone; the church is Christ’s own body, and he bears what it bears. The sobering truth is that how we treat our fellow believers is how we treat Christ.

Persons for one another

Bonhoeffer was fascinated by what it means to be a person. We become persons, he argued, only in relation — above all when we are confronted by another who is not ourselves, who stands before us with a claim we cannot simply absorb. The other person is a kind of boundary to me. I cannot make him into an extension of my own wishes. And in the church, that meeting with the other is taken up into God’s purpose. My brother is not only a boundary but a gift, and Christ meets me in him.

From this came a theme that ran through all his later work: members of Christ’s body stand in for one another. As Christ acted in our place, bearing our sin, so his people, in a lesser but real way, act for one another. Bonhoeffer named three ways in which this happens. We work for one another, giving up our own advantage for the good of the other. We pray for one another — and intercession, he said, is one of the most powerful acts of love in the church. And we forgive one another, declaring God’s forgiveness to each other in Christ’s name.

I exhort therefore, that, first of all, supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks, be made for all men. 1 TIMOTHY 2:1
And whether one member suffer, all the members suffer with it; or one member be honoured, all the members rejoice with it. 1 CORINTHIANS 12:26

This is not sentiment. It is a description of how the body actually works. When one member suffers, the others suffer too, whether they notice or not. When one prays, the others are carried. When one forgives, the whole body is healed a little.

The real church and the sinful church

Bonhoeffer was no romantic about the church. He knew it was full of sinners, including its ministers, and he wrote his dissertation in a German Protestant church that was already, in many places, lukewarm. How can a body so obviously flawed be Christ existing as community?

His answer was that the church is both at once. It is a real, historical, often disappointing human community, and it is at the same time the body of Christ. We do not find the true church by leaving the actual one in search of a purer version somewhere else. We find it by faith, in the midst of the actual one. The communion of saints is a communion of forgiven sinners. It is holy not because its members are impressive but because Christ is present in it.

Unto the church of God which is at Corinth, to them that are sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints. 1 CORINTHIANS 1:2

Paul wrote those words to the most troubled congregation in the New Testament — quarrelsome, immoral, proud and confused. And he called them saints. Not because they deserved it, but because Christ had claimed them.

What this changes

If the church is Christ existing as community, several things follow.

First, Christian faith is never merely private. There is no such thing as a solitary disciple who needs no one else. The individual believer is joined to others in Christ, whether he feels it or not.

Second, the local congregation — with its awkward members, its dull meetings and its unfinished business — is not to be despised. It is the place where Christ has chosen to be.

That they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee, that they also may be one in us: that the world may believe that thou hast sent me. JOHN 17:21

A caution

Some readers will hear in this language an echo of Roman Catholic or high-church teaching, which identifies Christ very closely with the institutional church. Bonhoeffer was a Lutheran, and he did not mean that the church is Christ in such a way that its decisions are Christ’s decisions or its hierarchy beyond question; the German church of the 1930s gave him ample reason to know otherwise. He meant that Christ is truly present among his people and gives himself to them in word and sacrament and in one another. The church remains under the word, not above it. Held in that way, his teaching can enrich Christians of every tradition.

From whom the whole body fitly joined together and compacted by that which every joint supplieth, according to the effectual working in the measure of every part, maketh increase of the body unto the edifying of itself in love. EPHESIANS 4:16
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Think of the congregation you belong to. Is it, in your mind, more like a club you have joined or a body into which you have been placed? What difference would the second make?

2. Choose three members of your church whom you do not know well. Pray for each of them by name every day this week.

3. Ask where one member of your church is suffering. Find one practical way to share that suffering.

4. If you have been drifting from the church because of its faults, bring those faults to God in prayer — and then go back.

5. Name one person in your church you need to forgive. Tell God, and if it is right, tell them.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You are the head of the body, and You have made me a member. I confess that I have often treated Your church as a club I could leave, or a service I could shop for.
Forgive me for despising those You have joined to me. Teach me to see You in my brothers and sisters, and to treat them as I would treat You.
Make me one who stands in for others — who works for them, prays for them, and forgives them in Your name.
And make Your church one, as You and the Father are one, that the world may believe that You were sent. Amen.

fields.title: The Visible Church
fields.body_html:
Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid. MATTHEW 5:14

The first part of Discipleship is about the call of Jesus to the individual. The second part, less often read, is about the church. Bonhoeffer knew that his teaching on the call could be misheard as a kind of heroic individualism — the lonely disciple, set apart from everyone, making his costly choices alone. That was not what he meant. The one who follows Jesus is never left alone. He is received into a company, a body, a people. And that people, Bonhoeffer insisted, is visible. It takes up room in the world.

Called into a body

In the Gospels the disciples could see Jesus and walk behind him on the road. How do we follow him now? Bonhoeffer’s answer was that Christ is present in his body, the church — in the word preached, in baptism and the Lord’s Supper, and in the fellowship of his people. We are not further from him than the first disciples; we meet him in the community he has gathered.

Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life. ROMANS 6:4

Bonhoeffer wrote about baptism as a break with the old life, a death and a new beginning, a call into Christ’s body. As a Lutheran he held to the baptism of infants, and many readers will differ from him on that. But on this point Christians of every tradition can agree with him: baptism is not a private religious ceremony but an entry into a people. It marks a person as belonging to Christ and to his church, publicly and irreversibly.

A people with a shape

A body, Bonhoeffer pointed out, takes up space. So does the church. It is not merely a set of shared beliefs or an invisible fellowship of souls. It has a place in the world, and it claims that place in three ways.

It claims space for the preaching of the word. Wherever the gospel is proclaimed, there is a public claim that Christ is Lord.

It claims space for worship and the sacraments — for a people gathered at the font and the table, visibly marked as belonging to him.

And it claims space for a common life. The early church, Bonhoeffer noted, did not merely believe together. It lived together. Its members shared their goods, ate together, cared for widows, and made room for one another across every line their world drew.

And all that believed were together, and had all things common; And sold their possessions and goods, and parted them to all men, as every man had need. ACTS 2:44–45

That shared life reached into the most ordinary relationships. When Paul sent the runaway slave Onesimus back to Philemon, he asked him to receive him not now as a servant, but above a servant, a brother beloved (Philemon 16). The old order was not abolished at a stroke; but within the church it was already broken open from within.

There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus. GALATIANS 3:28

Bonhoeffer wrote those pages at a time when the German state was demanding that the church exclude Christians of Jewish descent from its ministry. The visible church, as he understood it, could not accept that demand. A church that drew racial lines within its own body would cease to be the body of Christ.

A holy people

The church is not only visible but holy. Bonhoeffer spoke of the church-community of saints — not a society of the morally impressive, but a people set apart by God and called to live accordingly. That meant, among other things, that the church must care about how its members live. He wrote about church discipline, not as a harsh policing of the flock, but as the loving pursuit of a brother who has strayed.

Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted. GALATIANS 6:1

The point of discipline, as he understood it, is always restoration. It begins with a private word, spoken in humility; it moves only step by step towards anything more public; and it aims throughout at winning the brother back. A church that never speaks a word of correction is not being kind. It is leaving its members to face their sin alone.

Formed into his image

Discipleship ends with a chapter on the image of Christ. God made humanity in his own image; that image was defaced by sin; and God’s purpose in calling disciples is to restore it. The disciple does not become like Christ by imitating him from a distance. He becomes like Christ by being with him, by following him, and by being conformed to him — to the Christ who became man, was crucified and rose again.

For whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brethren. ROMANS 8:29

That is where the whole long argument of the book comes to rest. Costly grace, the call, the Sermon on the Mount, the visible church — all of it serves one end: that Christ might take form in his people.

But we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory, even as by the Spirit of the Lord. 2 CORINTHIANS 3:18

A hard edge

It should be said honestly that Bonhoeffer’s insistence on the visible church had a sharp edge in the 1930s. In the struggle between the Confessing Church and the Nazified church government, he argued that a Christian who knowingly separated himself from the Confessing Church was separating himself from the true church, and this drew strong objection even from his friends. Many readers will think he pressed the point too far. But the concern behind it is worth hearing. There are times when the church’s visible boundaries matter, because to blur them is to deny Christ. The German Christians who welcomed the regime’s demands into their church had shown what happens when they are blurred.

Let us go forth therefore unto him without the camp, bearing his reproach. For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come. HEBREWS 13:13–14

The visible church does not hide. It stands where it can be seen, and bears the consequences.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. How visible is your faith, and your church’s life, to the neighbourhood around you? Name one way your congregation takes up space in the world for Christ.

2. Are there lines in your church — of class, race, age or background — that the gospel has not yet crossed? Take one step across such a line this month.

3. If you are baptised, give thanks for it today as your public entry into Christ’s people. If you are not, ask what is holding you back.

4. Is there a brother or sister you have watched drift into sin and said nothing? Pray first; then, humbly and privately, speak.

5. Pray for Christians in places where to belong visibly to the church is costly.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You have not left Your disciples alone. You have gathered them into Your body, and You have set that body like a city on a hill.
Forgive me for wanting a private faith, hidden from the world and untroubled by my neighbours. Make me glad to be seen as Yours.
Break down within Your church the walls the world builds between people. Teach us to live together as brothers and sisters, sharing what we have.
Form Christ in us, until Your image is seen in Your people and the world knows that we are Your disciples by our love. Amen.

fields.title: A Gift, Not an Ideal
fields.body_html:
Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity! PSALM 133:1

When the Gestapo closed the Finkenwalde seminary in 1937, the experiment in common life that Bonhoeffer had led there was scattered. In the autumn of 1938, working in Göttingen, he wrote a short book about what they had learned. It was published in 1939 as Life Together, and it is the most practical, and perhaps the most widely loved, of all his writings. It begins not with a programme for Christian community but with gratitude.

A privilege, not a right

Bonhoeffer opened the book by reminding his readers that Christians living together is not to be taken for granted. Jesus himself lived in the midst of his enemies, and at the end all his disciples forsook him. Many Christians, in his own day and ours, live scattered — in prisons, in hostile places, among unbelievers, with no other believer near. For them the mere sight of another Christian face can be a great joy. The prisoner, the sick, the isolated missionary know this well. Those of us who can gather freely every week should not forget what a gift it is.

The LORD shall send the rod of thy strength out of Zion: rule thou in the midst of thine enemies. PSALM 110:2

Bonhoeffer wrote this as a man who knew that the freedom to gather could be taken away at any moment. It had already been taken from his seminary. Within a few years it would be taken from him. Most Christians who have ever lived have known that the fellowship of believers is precious precisely because it is fragile. The ones who forget are usually the ones who have never been without it.

Community through Christ

What makes Christian community Christian? Bonhoeffer answered: that it exists only through Jesus Christ and in him. We belong to one another not because we like one another, or share interests, or have chosen one another, but because Christ has made us his own. He is the mediator between us. I cannot reach my brother directly, as it were, by my own affection or effort; I reach him through Christ, and Christ reaches me through him.

This is why, Bonhoeffer said, the Christian needs other Christians. Left to himself, he is uncertain and easily deceived. His own heart wavers. But God has chosen to speak to him through the word of a brother or sister. When another believer speaks the gospel to me — tells me I am forgiven, reminds me of God’s promise — that word from outside is stronger than all the uncertain voices within. We need one another as bearers of God’s word.

For I long to see you, that I may impart unto you some spiritual gift, to the end ye may be established; That is, that I may be comforted together with you by the mutual faith both of you and me. ROMANS 1:11–12

Even Paul, the apostle, longed to be strengthened by the faith of ordinary believers in Rome. No Christian is so strong that he does not need to hear the gospel from someone else.

The death of the dream

Then comes the part of Life Together that has probably done more good in more congregations than anything else Bonhoeffer wrote. He warned against what might be called the dream of community — the picture of Christian fellowship that many believers carry in their heads before they have experienced the real thing. It is an ideal of warmth, harmony, depth and spiritual intensity. And sooner or later, he said, God shatters it.

The shattering is painful. We discover that our brothers and sisters are not what we imagined. They are dull, or irritating, or weak, or unspiritual. And so, we discover, are we. Bonhoeffer said that this disillusionment is a great mercy. The sooner it comes, the better, because only when the dream is dead can we receive the real community God has given. The real thing is not an ideal to be achieved but a reality to be accepted. It already exists, in Christ, and our task is to enter it with gratitude, not to construct it according to our own design.

Wherefore receive ye one another, as Christ also received us to the glory of God. ROMANS 15:7

He added a warning that many pastors have found almost unbearably accurate. The person who loves his dream of community more than the community itself, he said, will end by destroying it, however sincere he may be. He becomes a critic of his brothers, then an accuser, then an accuser of God. He comes to the fellowship with demands, sets up his own standards, and judges everyone by them. When they fail, he blames them; when the dream fails, he blames God. The community is not built up by such a person but slowly poisoned.

Who art thou that judgest another man’s servant? to his own master he standeth or falleth. ROMANS 14:4

Thankful for small things

The remedy Bonhoeffer offered was gratitude. We should thank God daily for the Christian fellowship we have been given, even when it is small, even when it is disappointing, even when there are no great experiences to speak of. A Christian who complains about his church, especially a pastor who complains about his congregation, should be careful. God did not give him that fellowship so that he might be its judge. He gave it so that he might love it.

I thank my God always on your behalf, for the grace of God which is given you by Jesus Christ. 1 CORINTHIANS 1:4

Paul wrote that to Corinth — the church that had given him more heartache than any other. He began not with complaint but with thanks, because he saw them first as the work of God’s grace.

Two kinds of love

Bonhoeffer drew one more distinction in this chapter, between what he called human love and spiritual love. Human love, in his sense, is the love that wants something from the other — desire, influence, closeness, the satisfaction of being needed. It can be very intense and look very spiritual. But at bottom it serves itself. It seeks to bind others to itself, to win them, to shape them. Spiritual love is different. It comes from Christ and serves the other for Christ’s sake. It respects the other’s freedom. It does not try to control or manipulate. It is content to bring the other to Christ and leave him there.

Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up, Doth not behave itself unseemly, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil. 1 CORINTHIANS 13:4–5

Real people, real grace

The whole chapter comes down to this: the fellowship God gives is made of real people, with all their faults, and it is held together by real grace, not by our ideals. We do not find perfect brothers. We find forgiven ones. And in accepting them as God has accepted us, we discover that the community we dreamed of was far smaller than the one God had prepared.

We know that we have passed from death unto life, because we love the brethren. 1 JOHN 3:14
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Thank God, specifically and by name, for three members of your church this week — especially one who irritates you.

2. Write down the picture of Christian community you carry in your head. Where has reality disappointed it? Offer both the picture and the disappointment to God.

3. If you have been a critic of your congregation, stop for a month. Speak no complaint about it to anyone but God.

4. Ask someone in your church to speak the gospel to you this week — to remind you of God’s forgiveness. Then do the same for someone else.

5. Examine one relationship where you have influence. Are you binding that person to yourself, or bringing them to Christ?

A PRAYER
Father, You have given me brothers and sisters I would not have chosen, and I have not always thanked You for them. Forgive me.
I have loved my dream of Your church more than Your church. I have judged those You have received. Break my ideal, and give me the real fellowship You have made in Christ.
Teach me to love as You love — not to possess or control, but to serve and to set free.
Thank You for every Christian face You have set before me. Keep me from ever taking that gift for granted. Amen.
