fields.title: The Day Together
fields.body_html:
My voice shalt thou hear in the morning, O LORD; in the morning will I direct my prayer unto thee, and will look up. PSALM 5:3

After the chapter on community, Life Together turns to something far more ordinary: how Christians who live together should spend a day. Bonhoeffer was writing from the experience of Finkenwalde, where young pastors shared a house, but he meant his counsel for Christian households of every kind — families, communities, anyone who shares a roof and a faith. What is striking about the chapter is how plain it is. There are no techniques, no spiritual athletics. There is a morning, a table, a day of work and an evening. And in each of them, the Word of God.

The day begins with God

Bonhoeffer thought the first moments of the day belong to God. Before the newspaper, before the plans, before the first worry, the Christian household should gather to hear the Word and to pray. The morning is not a time to be filled with our own thoughts, but to be quiet before the one who gives the day. Early Christians, he noted, felt the resurrection morning in every sunrise. The darkness is past; the light has come; the day belongs to the risen Lord.

It is of the LORD’s mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness. LAMENTATIONS 3:22–23

That common morning worship, as he described it, had several parts: the Psalms, the reading of Scripture, a hymn, and prayer. Each deserves a word.

Psalms, Scripture and song

The Psalms, he said, should be at the heart of the church’s common prayer, prayed together day after day. We shall come back to his teaching on the Psalms in a later chapter; here it is enough to say that he thought the church should learn to pray by praying the prayers God has given it.

Then comes Scripture. Bonhoeffer urged that it be read at length and consecutively — whole chapters from the Old and New Testaments, taken in order, day after day, rather than a verse or two chosen for the occasion. His reason is worth pondering. The Bible is not a collection of helpful sayings but a single great story of what God has done, above all in Jesus Christ. When we read it through, we are drawn into that story. We learn that our own lives are not the centre, and that the history which really matters is God’s history with his people. We find ourselves, he said, in the Bible, rather than trying to find the Bible in ourselves.

And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself. LUKE 24:27

He admitted that long readings would be hard for many modern Christians, who had lost the habit of listening. But he thought the loss was a sign of poverty, not maturity. A household that does not know the Bible cannot live by it.

Then song. Bonhoeffer loved music, and he had strong views on singing. He wanted the household to sing together, and he particularly valued singing in unison: one melody, one voice, the words carried by the tune rather than the tune showing off the singers. He was suspicious of any singing that drew attention to itself. The church sings, he said, not to perform but to join the song of the whole people of God, in heaven and on earth.

Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord. EPHESIANS 5:19

Praying for one another

After Scripture and song comes prayer, and here Bonhoeffer thought that someone in the household — often its head — should pray freely for the others, in his own words. This prayer should not be a sermon disguised as prayer, nor a display of piety. It should gather up the real needs, joys, sins and tasks of the household and bring them before God. Such praying is not easy. It requires knowing the others well, and it requires the one who prays to pray as one of them, not above them. But it binds a household together as few other things can.

The table

Then there is the table. Bonhoeffer gave a surprising amount of attention to meals. Jesus was known to his disciples in the breaking of bread; and every shared meal among Christians, he thought, carries something of that. We give thanks, because the food is a gift. We eat together, because God has made us a family. And we remember that there are others who are hungry, and that the bread we eat is not ours alone.

And it came to pass, as he sat at meat with them, he took bread, and blessed it, and brake, and gave to them. And their eyes were opened, and they knew him. LUKE 24:30–31

A family that eats together, gives thanks together and shares its bread with the stranger is already living out something of the gospel. Many modern households have lost the common meal altogether. Bonhoeffer would have counted that a real loss.

Work

After the morning comes the day’s work, and Bonhoeffer insisted that this too belongs to God. Prayer and work are not rivals. The monk’s old rule — pray and work — expresses the rhythm of Christian life. Work takes us out of ourselves and into the world of things, tasks and people. It disciplines us. It humbles us. And offered to God, it becomes a kind of prayer.

And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men. COLOSSIANS 3:23

He also thought that the morning’s prayer gives the day’s work its freedom. The Christian who has begun the day in God’s presence need not work anxiously. The day is already in God’s hands.

The evening

Finally, evening. Bonhoeffer counselled that the household gather again at the end of the day for prayer — and especially for forgiveness. Before sleep, Christians should ask pardon of God and of one another for the wrongs of the day. No quarrel should be carried into the night. The evening is a small rehearsal for the last evening, when we shall commit ourselves into God’s hands for good.

Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath. EPHESIANS 4:26
I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety. PSALM 4:8

Not a rulebook

It would be easy to read this chapter as a rigid timetable, and Bonhoeffer did not intend it so. A family with small children cannot live like a seminary. The point is the principle: a Christian household should let the Word of God shape its day, together, from morning to night, in whatever form suits it.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Look honestly at how your day begins. What claims your first attention? Give the first ten minutes of tomorrow to Scripture and prayer before anything else.

2. If you share a home with other believers, agree on one simple form of common prayer — even five minutes — and keep it for a month.

3. Begin reading one book of the Bible straight through, a chapter a day, rather than choosing verses at random.

4. Eat at least one meal this week with others, deliberately, giving thanks — and invite someone who would otherwise eat alone.

5. Before you sleep tonight, ask forgiveness of anyone you have wronged today, and of God.

A PRAYER
Lord, You give me each new day, and I have often filled it before I have given it back to You.
Teach me to begin in Your presence, to hear Your Word before any other word, and to pray before I plan.
Bless the tables where Your people eat together, and let us know You in the breaking of bread.
Make my work an offering to You. And when evening comes, let me lay down every quarrel, receive Your forgiveness, and sleep in peace, because You alone make me dwell in safety. Amen.

fields.title: The Day Alone
fields.body_html:
But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret; and thy Father which seeth in secret shall reward thee openly. MATTHEW 6:6

A book about Christian community might be expected to have little to say about solitude. Bonhoeffer gave it a whole chapter. Life Together moves from the day together to the day alone, and he insisted that the two cannot be separated. Why we need both

Why should a person who cannot bear solitude be wary of community? Because he may be using other people to escape himself. He seeks company not to love others but to avoid the silence in which he must face God. He fills every hour with talk and activity, and the fellowship becomes a noise that drowns out the voice he most needs to hear. Such a person brings his emptiness into the community and asks it to fill him. It cannot.

Why should a person who shuns community be wary of solitude? Because he may be using solitude to escape others. He retreats into his own spiritual life, cultivates his inner experience, and is answerable to no one. His solitude becomes a fortress of self-regard. Bonhoeffer thought that such a person was in danger of vanity and despair, cut off from the correction and comfort God gives through a brother.

Silence

The day alone begins with silence. Bonhoeffer did not mean an empty silence, or the kind of mystical stillness that seeks to empty the mind. He meant the silence of the one who waits to hear the Word of God. We are silent, he said, so that God may speak; and we are silent afterwards, so that his word may sink in. Silence and speech belong together. The one who has learned to be silent before God will speak more truly to others, and less.

He noticed how anxious many people are in silence. It feels empty, even threatening. We reach for noise. But he thought that learning to be silent before God was one of the great disciplines of the Christian life, and one that must simply be practised. It does not come naturally. It comes with time.

The heart of the day alone, for Bonhoeffer, was meditation on Scripture. This was not study, and it was not sermon preparation. The student was not to ask what the text meant for others, or how he might preach it. He was to ask what God was saying to him.

Do not try to cover it all or exhaust it; stay with a word or a phrase as long as it speaks. Accept the text as God’s word addressed to you today. Do not look for new ideas or striking experiences; often the time will seem dry, and that does not matter. What matters is that we have heard, and that the word goes with us into the day, as Mary kept the words she had heard and pondered them in her heart.

But Mary kept all these things, and pondered them in her heart. LUKE 2:19
Thy words were found, and I did eat them; and thy word was unto me the joy and rejoicing of mine heart. JEREMIAH 15:16

He admitted the difficulty. The mind wanders. Thoughts of the day’s work crowd in. His advice was not to fight them anxiously but to bring them into the prayer — to pray about the very thing that distracts us, and then return to the text. Patience, not strain, is the secret.

Prayer from the Word

Meditation, he said, leads naturally into prayer. The word we have heard becomes the word we pray. This keeps prayer from wandering into our own preoccupations; it gives it a shape and a direction that come from God rather than from ourselves. The Psalms are the great school of this kind of prayer, but any passage of Scripture can become the starting point.

O how love I thy law! it is my meditation all the day. PSALM 119:97

Intercession

Then Bonhoeffer turned to intercession — praying for others — and here he said something that many readers have found transforming. Intercession, he said, changes the one who prays. I cannot go on hating a brother for whom I pray. When I bring him before God, I see him as he is: a poor sinner, like me, in need of grace. His faults, which loomed so large, are seen in the light of the cross. And his needs, which I had overlooked, become my concern.

He added two practical points. Intercession should be specific: not a vague blessing on everyone, but particular people, with particular needs, by name. And it should be regular: a daily duty, not an occasional impulse. He thought that a Christian community in which every member prays daily for the others is held together by bonds stronger than any other. And he believed, too, that the one who is prayed for is truly helped — that intercession is not merely a pious exercise but real work, done before God, on another’s behalf.

How can we know whether our time alone is doing its work? Bonhoeffer offered a simple test. The fruit of the day alone should be seen in the day together. If our meditation makes us more patient with our brothers, more ready to serve, more willing to hear and to forgive, then it has been real. If it makes us proud of our spirituality, impatient with the less devout, or withdrawn from ordinary duties, then something has gone wrong. Solitude is not an end in itself. It is a preparation for love.

In the prison at Tegel he had solitude enough, and he kept the disciplines he had taught: Scripture, the Psalms, prayer for those he loved. The letters from that time show a man whose inner life had been formed long before the cell door closed.

3. Notice, too, where you use solitude to escape the demands of others. Who have you been avoiding?

4. Make a list of people to pray for by name, with specific needs. Pray through it daily for a month.

5. Choose one person you find difficult. Pray for them every day this week, and watch what happens in you.

Give me a word from Your Scripture each day, and let me keep it and ponder it in my heart as Mary did.
Teach me to pray for others, by name and with love, until I see them as You see them.
And let my time alone with You make me more patient, more humble, and more ready to love those You have given me. Amen.

fields.title: Listening and Bearing
fields.body_html:
Bear ye one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ. GALATIANS 6:2

The fourth chapter of Life Together is about service, and it begins, of all places, with an argument. On the road to Jerusalem the disciples fell to disputing which of them was the greatest. Bonhoeffer thought that the same question arises wherever Christians live together, usually unspoken. Who is the strongest here, the wisest, the most spiritual, the most important? The moment a group forms, the comparing begins. And the rest of the chapter is his answer to it: a series of plain, unglamorous ministries by which the members of a community serve one another instead of competing.

And there was also a strife among them, which of them should be accounted the greatest. LUKE 22:24

Holding the tongue

The first ministry Bonhoeffer named is the ministry of holding one’s tongue. It is the least spectacular thing imaginable, and perhaps the hardest. He meant, especially, refusing to speak about a brother behind his back — not only malicious gossip, but the casual criticism, the knowing remark, the story told to raise a laugh at another’s expense. He thought that a community in which this rule was kept would be transformed, and that one in which it was broken would slowly be poisoned.

Speak not evil one of another, brethren. JAMES 4:11

Meekness

The second ministry is meekness — not thinking too highly of oneself. Bonhoeffer thought that the Christian who truly knows his own sin will not be quick to rank himself above others. He will see his own failures more clearly than anyone else’s, because he knows them from the inside. He will not demand honour, and he will not be crushed when he is overlooked. Paul, near the end of his ministry, called himself the chief of sinners; Bonhoeffer took that as the posture of a mature Christian, not a morbid one.

This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief. 1 TIMOTHY 1:15

Listening

Then comes the ministry for which this chapter is best known: listening. The first service we owe to others, Bonhoeffer said, is to listen to them. God listens to us, and we are to do the same for our brothers. Yet Christians, and especially pastors, are always tempted to speak instead. We think that our job is to offer something — advice, correction, a word from Scripture — and so we half-listen, waiting for our turn. Many people are looking for an ear and do not find it among Christians, because Christians are too busy talking.

Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath. JAMES 1:19

He went further. The one who cannot listen to his brother, he warned, will soon find that he cannot listen to God either. He will be talking in God’s presence too. Listening is not a technique for counselling. It is a form of love, and a form of humility, and it is learned in the same school as prayer.

He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him. PROVERBS 18:13

Helping, even when interrupted

The fourth ministry is simple, practical help — active helpfulness in small, ordinary things. Bonhoeffer noticed how easily Christians excuse themselves from this because they have more important work to do. The priest and the Levite in the parable were very likely on their way to religious duties. They passed by. Bonhoeffer said that we must be ready to be interrupted by God, and that the interruptions often come in the form of someone who needs a hand. The Christian who is too busy with his spiritual schedule to help a neighbour has missed the point of the schedule.

And by chance there came down a certain priest that way: and when he saw him, he passed by on the other side. LUKE 10:31

This is a humbling word for anyone whose days are full of worthy things. The interruption we resent may be the most important appointment of the day.

Bearing

The fifth ministry is bearing one another, and here Bonhoeffer went deepest. To bear a brother is first to put up with him — to endure his peculiarities, his weaknesses, his way of doing things. It is to allow him his freedom, even when his freedom annoys us. The strong must bear with the weak; but everyone is weak in some way, and so everyone must be borne.

We then that are strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak, and not to please ourselves. ROMANS 15:1

But bearing goes further still. It means bearing the other’s sin — not excusing it, but forgiving it, again and again, as Christ bore our sin on the cross. Bonhoeffer saw this as the very heart of the Christian community. God bore with us; Christ carried our sins; and those who have been borne are called to bear. A community that will only include the easy and the agreeable has not understood the gospel.

Forbearing one another, and forgiving one another, if any man have a quarrel against any: even as Christ forgave you, so also do ye. COLOSSIANS 3:13

Speaking the word, and true authority

Only after all these ministries did Bonhoeffer come to the ministry of speaking — telling a brother God’s word of comfort, warning or forgiveness. He thought such speaking was essential, but that it had to grow out of the listening, the bearing and the humility that came before. A word spoken without them would be cheap, and would not be heard. Spoken with them, it could be God’s own word to a brother in need.

He ended with a word about authority. True authority in the church, he said, is the authority of service; the church should be wary of dazzling personalities who gather followers around themselves. That was a pointed warning in a Germany that had given itself to a leader, and it remains pointed wherever the church celebrates its celebrities.

But so shall it not be among you: but whosoever will be great among you, shall be your minister. MARK 10:43
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. For one week, speak no criticism of any fellow Christian who is not present. If something needs saying, say it to them.

2. In your next three conversations, listen until the other person has finished, without planning your reply. Ask one more question than you normally would.

3. Notice the interruptions in your day this week. Treat at least one as an appointment from God.

4. Name one person whose ways irritate you. Ask God to help you bear with them, and do one kind thing for them.

5. If you hold any position of influence in your church, ask whether people are being drawn to you or to Christ.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You came not to be served but to serve, and You bore my sins on the cross. Forgive me for comparing, ranking and competing with those You have made my brothers.
Set a guard over my tongue. Teach me to listen as You listen to me, and to be interrupted without resentment.
Give me grace to bear with others as You have borne with me — their weakness, their freedom and their sin.
Make me a servant, and let whatever authority I have point away from me to You. Amen.

fields.title: Confession to One Another
fields.body_html:
Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed. The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much. JAMES 5:16

Life Together ends with a chapter on confession and the Lord’s Supper, and it is the part of the book that many Protestant readers find most surprising. Bonhoeffer believed that Christians should confess their sins not only to God in private but to one another — to a brother or sister in Christ, face to face. At Finkenwalde this was not a theory. It was practised. It was also, by the testimony of those who were there, one of the most difficult and most fruitful things they did together.

The lonely fellowship

Bonhoeffer began with a diagnosis. Many Christian fellowships, he observed, are lonely places. Their members pray together, sing together, study together — and remain utterly alone with their sins. Everyone assumes that everyone else is getting on well. Everyone hides. The fellowship is pious, but it is a fellowship of the pious, not of sinners, and no one is allowed to be a sinner in it. So each member carries his real failures in secret, and the more he hides them the more alone he becomes.

When I kept silence, my bones waxed old through my roaring all the day long. For day and night thy hand was heavy upon me. PSALM 32:3–4

The gospel cuts through that loneliness. It tells us that we are sinners, all of us, and that God loves sinners. In Christ we are free to be what we are before God. And if we are free to be sinners before God, Bonhoeffer asked, why should we not be free to be sinners before one another?

Four breakthroughs

He described confession to a brother as a series of breakthroughs.

It is a breakthrough to community. Sin wants to be alone. It isolates, it hides, it withdraws. The more secret it is, the stronger its grip. When it is spoken aloud to a brother, it loses much of its power. The one who confesses is no longer alone with it; he has come into the light, and into fellowship.

But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship one with another, and the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin. 1 JOHN 1:7

It is a breakthrough to the cross. Pride is the root of sin, and nothing humbles pride like confessing a specific sin to another person. It is a kind of death. We would much rather confess to God alone, where no one else sees. Bonhoeffer thought that the humiliation of confession to a brother was a share in the humiliation of Christ, who was exposed and shamed on the cross for us.

It is a breakthrough to new life. Confession is a turning point. The past is broken with; the sin is named and renounced; the forgiven one goes on in freedom. Bonhoeffer linked confession closely to discipleship: it is a way of leaving the old life behind and following Christ into the new.

He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy. PROVERBS 28:13

And it is a breakthrough to certainty. This is perhaps the most practical point of all. Why, Bonhoeffer asked, is it so often easier to confess to God than to a brother? Perhaps because, when we confess to God alone, we are really confessing to ourselves and forgiving ourselves. We have no one outside us to tell us the truth or to declare the forgiveness. And so we are never quite sure. When a brother hears our confession and speaks God’s forgiveness to us, in Christ’s name, we hear it from outside. The word of pardon is real, spoken, concrete. We can believe it.

If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness. 1 JOHN 1:9

Who should hear

To whom should we confess? Bonhoeffer was clear that this is not the privilege of an ordained priest. Any Christian can hear the confession of another, because every Christian has been given the ministry of reconciliation. What is needed is not a title but a person who lives beneath the cross himself — who knows the depth of his own sin and the greatness of God’s mercy. Such a person will not be shocked by anything he hears, because he knows what is in his own heart. He added a sobering rule: the one who does not himself confess should not hear the confession of others. Only those who have been humbled can be trusted with another’s humiliation.

And all things are of God, who hath reconciled us to himself by Jesus Christ, and hath given to us the ministry of reconciliation. 2 CORINTHIANS 5:18

It is worth adding what the wider Protestant tradition has always said. The one who hears a confession does not forgive sins by his own authority, nor is confession to another believer required for God’s forgiveness. God forgives the penitent sinner who comes to him through Christ. What the brother does is declare that forgiveness, pray, and stand with the one who confesses. That, Bonhoeffer thought, is gift enough.

The dangers

fields.title: The Prayer Book of the Bible
fields.body_html:
And it came to pass, that, as he was praying in a certain place, when he ceased, one of his disciples said unto him, Lord, teach us to pray, as John also taught his disciples. LUKE 11:1

In 1940 Bonhoeffer published a very short book on the Psalms. It was the last book he saw into print. In English it has appeared as Psalms: The Prayer Book of the Bible, and it can be read in an hour. It was written at a time when the Old Testament was being scorned in Germany as a Jewish book unfit for Christians, and it drew the disapproval of the authorities. Its argument is simple, and it has taught many Christians to pray.

Learning to pray

Bonhoeffer began with the disciples’ request: Lord, teach us to pray. They had been praying all their lives, as devout Jews did; and yet, watching Jesus, they knew they did not know how. Bonhoeffer thought this is where every Christian must begin. Prayer does not come naturally. We assume that it is simply pouring out our hearts to God. But the heart, left to itself, pours out wishes, fears, complaints and confusion. It does not know how to pray, as Paul says plainly.

Likewise the Spirit also helpeth our infirmities: for we know not what we should pray for as we ought: but the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered. ROMANS 8:26

How then do we learn? Bonhoeffer used a homely picture. A child learns to speak because his father speaks to him. He learns his father’s language by hearing it and repeating it. So it is with prayer. We learn to speak to God by hearing God speak to us, and by praying back to him the words he has given. That is why the Bible contains a book of prayers. God has given us, in the Psalms, the words with which to answer him.

God’s word and our prayer

This raises a puzzle, which Bonhoeffer faced squarely. The Bible is God’s word to us. The Psalms are human prayers to God. How can they be both? How can the words of David, crying out in distress or joy, be the word of God?

His answer was that the Psalms are, first of all, the prayer of Jesus Christ. Christ, the true Son of David, prayed these psalms during his earthly life. He took them on his lips in the synagogue, in the Temple, on the road — and on the cross. My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? is the first line of Psalm 22. Into thine hand I commit my spirit is from Psalm 31. The Psalter was the prayer book of Jesus. And because Christ prays it, it is at once the word of God and the prayer of man — for he is both.

Into thine hand I commit my spirit: thou hast redeemed me, O LORD God of truth. PSALM 31:5
And when Jesus had cried with a loud voice, he said, Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit: and having said thus, he gave up the ghost. LUKE 23:46

And because Christ prays it, his church can pray it with him. We pray the Psalms not merely as our own words but as members of his body, joining our voices to his. That is why Bonhoeffer thought the Psalms belong especially to the church’s common prayer. They are the prayer of the whole Christ, head and members together.

Praying what we do not feel

This has an immediate practical consequence. Many of the Psalms do not match our feelings on a given day. We are cheerful, and the psalm is a lament. We are grieving, and the psalm is a shout of praise. We feel innocent, and the psalm confesses sin; we feel guilty, and the psalm protests innocence. Bonhoeffer said that this is exactly as it should be. The Psalms are not the expression of our moods. They are the prayer of Christ and his whole church, and on any given day someone in that church is weeping and someone is rejoicing. When we pray a psalm that does not fit our mood, we pray for and with those whose mood it does fit. And we learn to pray beyond ourselves.

Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted in me? hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him for the help of his countenance. PSALM 42:5

The hard psalms

What of the psalms that seem impossible to pray — the psalms of innocence, where the psalmist protests his righteousness, and the psalms of vengeance, where he calls down curses on his enemies?

Judge me, O LORD; for I have walked in mine integrity: I have trusted also in the LORD; therefore I shall not slide. PSALM 26:1

Bonhoeffer answered both from the same centre. The psalms of innocence are true, first of all, of Christ, the only truly innocent one. We pray them in him, as those clothed in his righteousness.

For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him. 2 CORINTHIANS 5:21

The psalms of vengeance he handled with great care. He did not soften them, nor did he treat them as sub-Christian outbursts to be skipped. He noted, first, that the psalmist does not take vengeance himself; he hands it over to God. That is already a great act of faith. Secondly, the enemies in these psalms are the enemies of God and his cause, not merely private rivals. And thirdly — this was his deepest point — God’s vengeance on sin has been carried out. It fell on Christ at the cross. The one who prays these psalms in Christ knows that the judgement he asks for has been borne by the Son, who prayed for his own enemies as he died.

Then said Jesus, Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do. LUKE 23:34

So the Christian may pray even these psalms, not in personal hatred, but in the longing for God’s justice to be done and for evil to be ended — and in the knowledge that the justice of God has been satisfied at the cross, so that enemies too may be forgiven.

Not every reader will find this answer fully satisfying, and there are other ways Christians have handled these texts. But Bonhoeffer’s refusal to cut them out, and his insistence on reading them through the cross, is a wise guide.

The whole of life

Bonhoeffer ended the book by setting out the great themes of the Psalter: creation, the law, the history of God’s people, the Messiah, the church, life, suffering, guilt, enemies and the end. The Psalms, he showed, cover the whole of human life before God. There is nothing we can experience that they do not bring into prayer. And so he urged that Christians pray them regularly, daily, as the church has done for centuries.

Seven times a day do I praise thee because of thy righteous judgments. PSALM 119:164
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Begin praying one psalm a day, aloud, in order, starting with Psalm 1. Pray it, do not merely read it.

2. When a psalm does not fit your mood, pray it for someone whose mood it does fit — someone grieving, rejoicing, afraid or guilty.

3. Read Psalm 22 alongside the account of the crucifixion in Matthew 27. Notice how Christ prayed the Psalms.

4. Choose one psalm of lament and pray it on behalf of Christians suffering persecution today.

5. If you find a psalm of vengeance hard to pray, pray it slowly while looking at the cross, and then pray for your own enemies.

A PRAYER
Lord, teach me to pray. I do not know how, and my own heart speaks mostly of itself.
Thank You for the words You have given, the prayers of Your Son and of Your people through the ages. Let me learn Your language by speaking it back to You.
When the psalm does not match my mood, let me pray with those whose mood it does match, and so pray beyond myself.
Lord Jesus, You prayed these psalms on earth and pray for me still. Take my poor prayers into Yours, and bring them to the Father. Amen.

fields.title: The Church for Others
fields.body_html:
For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many. MARK 10:45

In the spring of 1944, in his cell at Tegel, Bonhoeffer began to write to his friend Eberhard Bethge about ideas he had not yet worked out. They came in letters, in fragments, often late at night, with the sound of air raids overhead. He was trying to think through what Christian faith would look like in a world that no longer seemed to need God. These letters have become some of the most discussed pages in twentieth-century theology, and some of the most misused. This chapter tries to set out what he was reaching for, honestly and with care — and to draw out the one idea from them that every Christian can take hold of: the church that exists for others.

A world come of age

Bonhoeffer observed that the modern world had learned to manage without God in one area of life after another. Science, politics, medicine, ethics — each had found its own way of working that did not appeal to God to explain things or fill the gaps. He called this, in a phrase that has become famous, a world come of age. He did not mean that the world had become wiser or better. The war raging around him made that absurd. He meant that people had grown used to living as if God were not needed for the running of things.

How had the church responded? Too often, he thought, by retreating to the gaps — the places where human knowledge and strength ran out. God became the answer to the questions science had not yet answered, the comfort at the deathbed, the rescuer in the crisis. But as the gaps shrank, so did God. Bonhoeffer thought this was a betrayal. God is not a stopgap, brought in only at the boundaries of life when our own resources fail. He is the Lord at the centre of life — in our strength as well as our weakness, in our health as well as our sickness, in our daily work as well as our dying.

For in him we live, and move, and have our being. ACTS 17:28

That much, most Christians can gladly affirm. The God of the Bible is not a God of the gaps, but the Creator and Lord of all.

Religionless Christianity

Bonhoeffer went further, and here the reader must go carefully. He wondered aloud whether the time of religion was passing — and whether Christianity might need to be expressed in a non-religious way. By religion he did not mean faith in God, or worship, or prayer. He meant a particular way of being Christian that he had come to distrust: an inward, private, otherworldly piety that treats God as a means of meeting our needs and escaping the world. He wondered how the great words of the Bible — repentance, faith, justification, rebirth, sanctification — might be spoken in ways that addressed people in the midst of their lives rather than only at the edges.

He never answered his own question. He died before he could. But two things must be said about what he did write.

First, in the very same letters he insisted on what he called a secret discipline — the hidden life of prayer, worship and sacrament that the church must guard and practise, even when it cannot speak freely to the world. And he wrote that, for the time being, Christian existence would consist chiefly in two things: prayer, and doing what is right among people. A man who says that is not abandoning faith in God. He is stripping it to its core.

He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God? MICAH 6:8

Second, after his death some theologians took up his phrases and used them for their own ends. In the 1960s his prison letters were quoted in support of a Christianity without a personal God, and even of the claim that God was dead. That use of his work goes against everything else he wrote, and against the life he lived — a life of daily prayer, Scripture and worship, right up to the service he led on the day before his death. Readers should know that these fragments have been bent this way, and should read them in the light of the whole man.

The man for others

In the summer of 1944 Bonhoeffer sketched the outline of a book he hoped to write. It was never written, but the outline survives, and it contains the idea that gives this chapter its title. He described Jesus as the man for others — the one whose whole existence was given away for the sake of others, even to death. That self-giving, he said, is where we meet the transcendence of God: not in some remote power beyond the world, but in the one who was wholly for us.

For ye know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that, though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich. 2 CORINTHIANS 8:9

And from that followed his description of the church. The church, he wrote, is truly the church only when it exists for others. It must share in the ordinary life of the world, not dominating it but helping and serving. It must tell people of every calling what it means to live with Christ, to exist for others. He even suggested, in his outline, that the church should give away its wealth to those in need, and that its ministers should live on the free gifts of their congregations and perhaps work at ordinary callings.

Silver and gold have I none; but such as I have give I thee: In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth rise up and walk. ACTS 3:6

A church that serves

Whatever one makes of the prison fragments, this central idea is deeply biblical. The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve. The church, his body, must share his shape. It does not exist to preserve itself, to grow its influence or to secure its comfort. It exists to worship God and to serve the world for Christ’s sake — to bear witness, to heal, to feed, to comfort, to stand beside the suffering.

Hereby perceive we the love of God, because he laid down his life for us: and we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren. 1 JOHN 3:16

There is, of course, a danger on the other side. A church that exists only for others, and forgets that it exists first for God, becomes a charity with hymns. Bonhoeffer knew that; the secret discipline of prayer and worship was meant to guard against it. The church is for others because it is first for Christ. Its service flows from its worship, and not the other way round.

For we preach not ourselves, but Christ Jesus the Lord; and ourselves your servants for Jesus’ sake. 2 CORINTHIANS 4:5

That is the balance: Christ Jesus the Lord, and ourselves your servants. Hold both, and the church is what it should be.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Where do you treat God as a stopgap, turning to Him only when your own resources run out? Invite Him into the parts of life where you feel strong.

2. Ask how your church spends its money and time. How much goes to maintaining itself, and how much to serving others? Raise the question gently with those who lead.

3. Name one person or group in your neighbourhood that your church could serve. Take one step towards doing it.

4. Guard your own secret discipline — daily prayer, Scripture and worship — as the source of any service you give.

5. Read Philippians 2:1–11 and ask what it would mean for you, this week, to be a person for others.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You were the man for others, rich but made poor for our sake, serving to the end. Forgive Your church when it has lived for itself.

MARK 10:45 In the spring of 1944, in his cell at Tegel, Bonhoeffer began to write to his friend Eberhard Bethge about ideas he had not yet worked out. They came in letters, in fragments, often late at night, with the sound of air raids overhead. He was trying to think through what Christian faith would look like in a world that no longer seemed to need God. These letters have become some of the most discussed pages in twentieth-century theology, and some of the most misused. This chapter tries to set out what he was reaching for, honestly and with care — and to draw out the one idea from them that every Christian can take hold of: the church that exists for others. A world come of age Bonhoeffer observed that the modern world had learned to manage without God in one area of life after another. Science, politics, medicine, ethics — each had found its own way of working that did not appeal to God to explain things or fill the gaps. He called this, in a phrase that has become famous, a world come of age. He did not mean that the world had become wiser or better. The war raging around him made that absurd. He meant that people had grown used to living as if God were not needed for the running of things. How had the church responded? Too often, he thought, by retreating to the gaps — the places where human knowledge and strength ran out. God became the answer to the questions science had not yet answered, the comfort at the deathbed, the rescuer in the crisis. But as the gaps shrank, so did God. Guard your own secret discipline — daily prayer, Scripture and worship — as the source of any service you give. 5. fields.title: Responsibility and Guilt
fields.body_html:
If thou forbear to deliver them that are drawn unto death, and those that are ready to be slain; If thou sayest, Behold, we knew it not; doth not he that pondereth the heart consider it? PROVERBS 24:11–12

Between 1940 and his arrest in 1943, Bonhoeffer worked on the book he regarded as his life’s main task: an Ethics. He never finished it. What survives is a collection of drafts and fragments, some polished and some rough, which Eberhard Bethge gathered and published after the war. They were written by a man who was at the same time carrying messages for a conspiracy against the head of his own state. That makes them both more urgent and more difficult to read than anything else he wrote. This chapter sets out the heart of his teaching on responsibility, and then turns, as honestly as it can, to the question every reader asks: was he right to join the plot?

One reality

Bonhoeffer began his Ethics by rejecting a way of thinking he believed had crippled the church. Christians, he thought, had come to divide life into two realms — the sacred and the secular, the spiritual and the worldly, the church and the state — each with its own rules. The Christian lived in the first on Sundays and in the second the rest of the week, and the gospel had little to say about the second. Bonhoeffer insisted that in Jesus Christ God and the world have been reconciled, and that there is therefore only one reality: the reality of God made known in Christ, which embraces the whole world. There is no area of life where Christ is not Lord, and no area where the Christian may leave him behind.

And he is before all things, and by him all things consist. COLOSSIANS 1:17

Christ taking form

Ethics, for Bonhoeffer, was not first of all a set of rules but the question of how Christ takes form in his people in the real situations where they must act. The Christian does not ask what is good in general, but what God wills for him here and now, in the light of Christ — a patient, humble discernment rooted in Scripture and prayer.

My little children, of whom I travail in birth again until Christ be formed in you. GALATIANS 4:19

He also distinguished what he called the ultimate and the penultimate. The ultimate is God’s final word of grace in Christ — justification, the last and decisive word over every life. The penultimate is everything that comes before it: the ordinary human world of bread, justice, freedom, health. The penultimate is not the gospel, but it matters, because it prepares the way. A hungry man must be fed; a slave must be freed; a wronged man must have justice. Christians who care only about the ultimate and ignore the penultimate have misunderstood both.

The shape of responsible life

At the centre of the Ethics is a long section on what Bonhoeffer called responsible life. He described it in several strands. The responsible person acts for others, standing in their place, as Christ stood in ours. He acts in accordance with reality, not with an abstract ideal; he looks at the actual situation and the actual neighbour. He acts freely, not sheltering behind rules or orders, but answering for his own decision before God. And — this was the hardest part — he must sometimes be willing to take guilt upon himself.

Bonhoeffer argued that there are situations in which every choice is stained. To do nothing is itself a choice, and may be a guilty one. The man who keeps his own hands clean while others suffer has not escaped responsibility; he has only chosen his own innocence over his neighbour’s life. Christ, he said, did not stand aloof from human guilt, but took it upon himself for our sake. The responsible Christian may, in extreme circumstances, have to act in a way that incurs guilt, for the sake of others — and then he must not justify himself, but cast himself on the grace of God.

Therefore to him that knoweth to do good, and doeth it not, to him it is sin. JAMES 4:17

He also wrote movingly, in these pages, about the guilt of the church. The church, he said, must confess its own failure: its silence when it should have spoken, its cowardice before the powerful, its failure to defend the defenceless — above all the Jewish people who were being persecuted and murdered. That confession was written in the middle of the war, by a man who had tried to speak.

We have sinned, and have committed iniquity, and have done wickedly, and have rebelled, even by departing from thy precepts and from thy judgments. DANIEL 9:5

The conspiracy

Now to the question that cannot be avoided. Bonhoeffer, who a decade earlier had come close to Christian pacifism, lent his support to men who were planning to kill the head of state. How should Christians judge this?

Those who believe he was right point to the extremity of the situation. A regime was murdering the Jews of Europe, the sick and the disabled, and millions of others; it had waged aggressive war and was still waging it; there were no lawful means left to stop it. They point to a long Christian tradition, going back to the Middle Ages and the Reformation, which held that a tyrant who makes war on his own people may be resisted. They point to the Scriptures that command us to deliver those who are drawn to death, and to the Hebrew midwives who defied Pharaoh. And they note that Bonhoeffer never claimed that the plot was righteous. He called it a guilt, and he accepted it as such.

But the midwives feared God, and did not as the king of Egypt commanded them, but saved the men children alive. EXODUS 1:17

Those who believe he was wrong, or who are unsure, have serious arguments too. They point to Romans 13, which calls the governing authority the minister of God and forbids resisting it. They point to his own teaching in Discipleship, that the disciple overcomes evil by suffering rather than by force. They note that the midwives disobeyed, but did not kill. They note that the conspirators themselves had mixed motives, and that some had served the regime for years. And they warn that Bonhoeffer’s example has since been claimed to justify violence in causes he would never have supported.

Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God. ROMANS 13:1

This book will not pretend to settle the question. Faithful Christians have come down on both sides, and some have stayed in honest uncertainty. But three things can be said with confidence. First, Bonhoeffer did not reach his decision lightly, or without prayer, or out of hatred. Second, he did not treat it as a precedent or a principle for others to follow; he treated it as a terrible exception, carried out under a guilt that only grace could cover. Third, no one living in a free country, with lawful means of opposing wrong, can claim his example as a warrant for their own violence. Whatever the Ethics permits, it permits only in the last extremity, and it never calls it clean.

Forgiveness for the responsible

The Ethics ends where all of Bonhoeffer’s theology ends: in grace. The responsible person who acts and incurs guilt does not stand before God on the merit of his choice. He stands, like every sinner, on the mercy of Christ.

If thou, LORD, shouldest mark iniquities, O Lord, who shall stand? But there is forgiveness with thee, that thou mayest be feared. PSALM 130:3–4
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Where have you divided your life into sacred and secular? Choose one secular area — your work, your money, your politics — and ask what it would mean for Christ to be Lord there.

2. Is there a situation in which you have kept your own hands clean while someone else paid the price? What would responsibility require?

3. Name one penultimate need in your community — food, justice, safety — and do something about it.

4. Read Romans 13:1–7 and Acts 5:29 side by side. Pray for wisdom to know how to honour authority and when to obey God rather than men.

5. Pray for Christians who live under tyranny today, and who must make decisions you will never face.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus Christ, You are Lord of all things, and there is no part of the world where You are not King. Forgive me for keeping You in a corner of my life.
Give me courage to act responsibly for others, and not to shelter behind my own innocence when my neighbour is in need.
Where every choice is hard, give me wisdom. Where I have acted and been wrong, give me grace to confess it without excuse.
Forgive Your church for its silences. And let every one of us, whatever we have done or failed to do, find refuge in Your mercy alone. Amen.

fields.title: Suffering with God
fields.body_html:
Then saith he unto them, My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death: tarry ye here, and watch with me. MATTHEW 26:38

A prisoner has time to think about suffering. In Tegel, Bonhoeffer was surrounded by it — his own, his fellow prisoners’, the city’s under the bombs, and behind all of it the vast suffering of a continent at war. He did not write about it as a detached theologian. He wrote as a man who was himself afraid, separated from those he loved, uncertain whether he would live. And some of the most searching things he ever wrote concern the question every sufferer asks: where is God in this?

The God who is pushed out

In the summer of 1944, Bonhoeffer wrote to Bethge a thought that has been much quoted and much debated. God, he said, lets himself be pushed out of the world and onto the cross. He is weak and powerless in the world, and precisely in that way he is with us and helps us. Christ helps us not by his almighty power, as the world expects a god to help, but by his weakness and his suffering. And then came the phrase for which this letter is remembered: that only a suffering God can help.

What did he mean? He was not denying God’s power or sovereignty; the same letters are full of trust in God’s providence. He was pointing to the cross. The world looks for a god who will rescue it from above, a god of power who intervenes to set things right. The God of the Bible has come down into the world’s suffering in the person of his Son and borne it himself. The help he gives is not the help of a distant ruler but of one who has been where we are.

He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief: and we hid as it were our faces from him; he was despised, and we esteemed him not. ISAIAH 53:3
In all their affliction he was afflicted, and the angel of his presence saved them: in his love and in his pity he redeemed them. ISAIAH 63:9

Some readers from the classical tradition will be cautious about language of a suffering God, since the church has long taught that God in his own being is not subject to change or passion. That caution is worth keeping. Bonhoeffer’s phrase is best read as he meant it: as a statement about the cross, where the eternal Son truly suffered in the flesh. God has not remained untouched by our suffering. In Christ he has entered it, and borne it, and overcome it.

Standing by God

In another piece written in prison, a short poem, Bonhoeffer drew a contrast between two ways of turning to God. All people, he observed, go to God when they are in trouble, asking for help, bread, comfort and forgiveness. That is natural and right. But Christians do something more. They go to God when he is in trouble — they stand by him in his suffering, as the disciples were asked to watch with Christ in Gethsemane.

And he cometh unto the disciples, and findeth them asleep, and saith unto Peter, What, could ye not watch with me one hour? MATTHEW 26:40

This is a striking thought. We usually think of prayer as asking God to share in our troubles. Bonhoeffer asked his readers to consider sharing in his. Christ still suffers — in his body, the church, and in the least of his brothers. To be a Christian, in part, is to be drawn into that suffering, to watch with Christ, to refuse to sleep while he is in anguish.

That I may know him, and the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings, being made conformable unto his death. PHILIPPIANS 3:10

Living fully in this world

On 21 July 1944 — the day after the failed attempt on Hitler’s life, when he must have known what its failure meant for him — Bonhoeffer wrote a letter that many consider the most personal of all. He looked back on his own younger ambition to live a holy life, and on a conversation years before with a fellow pastor who had wanted to become a saint. He now saw, he wrote, that faith is not learned by cultivating one’s own holiness, but by giving up the project of making something of oneself and living wholeheartedly in the world as it is, with all its tasks and its failures, its muddle and its helplessness. The one who does that, and simply entrusts himself to God, stops being preoccupied with his own troubles and begins to share in God’s suffering in the world. That, Bonhoeffer thought, is what faith and repentance actually look like.

This is not the otherworldly piety he distrusted, nor a worldly activism without God. It is the life of a disciple who has stopped trying to be impressive and simply lives, day by day, in the world God has given, trusting and obeying, watching with Christ. It is striking that he wrote it on that particular day.

And if children, then heirs; heirs of God, and joint-heirs with Christ; if so be that we suffer with him, that we may be also glorified together. ROMANS 8:17

Who am I

Among his prison poems is one that has moved many readers: a meditation on the question of who he really was. Those around him in prison saw a man who seemed composed, cheerful and steady. Inwardly he knew fear, weariness and a hunger for freedom and friendship. Which was the real man — the one others saw, or the one he knew from the inside? He could not tell, and he did not pretend to.

He ended the poem not with an answer but with a turning to God. What he could not settle by looking inward was settled by belonging: he was known by God, and he was God’s.

O LORD, thou hast searched me, and known me. Thou knowest my downsitting and mine uprising, thou understandest my thought afar off. PSALM 139:1–2

Every sufferer knows the gap between the face shown to others and the fear inside. Bonhoeffer did not pretend it away. He handed it over.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. When you next suffer, ask not only for relief but for the grace to share in Christ’s sufferings. Read Philippians 3:7–11 slowly.

2. Where is Christ suffering in your neighbourhood today — in the poor, the sick, the imprisoned, the persecuted? Go and watch with Him there.

3. Stop trying to make something of yourself this week. Throw yourself into the ordinary duties in front of you, trusting God with the outcome.

4. Write down honestly the gap between how others see you and what you feel inside. Pray Psalm 139 over it.

5. Write to someone who is suffering, and share with them the comfort God has given you.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You were a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief. You did not rescue us from a distance; You came down and bore our suffering Yourself.
Forgive me for coming to You only when I am in trouble. Teach me to watch with You, and not to sleep while You are in anguish in Your people.
Where I cannot tell who I really am, remind me that You know me, and that I am Yours.
Teach me to live fully in the world You have given, throwing myself into Your arms, and to comfort others with the comfort You have given me. Amen.

That, Bonhoeffer thought, is what faith and repentance actually look like. This is not the otherworldly piety he distrusted, nor a worldly activism without God. It is the life of a disciple who has stopped trying to be impressive and simply lives, day by day, in the world God has given, trusting and obeying, watching with Christ. What he could not settle by looking inward was settled by belonging: he was known by God, and he was God’s. O LORD, thou hast searched me, and known me. Thou knowest my downsitting and mine uprising, thou understandest my thought afar off. PSALM 139:1–2 Every sufferer knows the gap between the face shown to others and the fear inside. Read Philippians 3:7–11 slowly. 2. Where is Christ suffering in your neighbourhood today — in the poor, the sick, the imprisoned, the persecuted? Go and watch with Him there. 3. Stop trying to make something of yourself this week. Throw yourself into the ordinary duties in front of you, trusting God with the outcome. 4. Write down honestly the gap between how others see you and what you feel inside. Pray Psalm 139 over it. 5. Write to someone who is suffering, and share with them the comfort God has given you. A PRAYER Lord Jesus, You were a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief. You did not rescue us from a distance; You came down and bore our suffering Yourself. Forgive me for coming to You only when I am in trouble. Teach me to watch with You, and not to sleep while You are in anguish in Your people. Where I cannot tell who I really am, remind me that You know me, and that I am Yours. Teach me to live fully in the world You have given, throwing myself into Your arms, and to comfort others with the comfort You have given me. Amen.

fields.title: The Beginning of Life
fields.body_html:
O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory? The sting of death is sin; and the strength of sin is the law. But thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ. 1 CORINTHIANS 15:55–57

Bonhoeffer’s life ended at dawn in a concentration camp, at the hands of a regime that was days from collapse. Nothing about the manner of it was dignified or just. And yet the Christians who have read his story have almost always come away from it not in despair but in hope. That is not because his death was made to look noble in the retelling, but because of what he believed, and wrote, and apparently said, about what lay on the other side of it. This last teaching chapter is about that hope.

Hope that sends us back

It is worth beginning with something Bonhoeffer said that may surprise readers. In his prison letters he warned against a certain kind of Christian hope — one that treats the next world as an escape from this one, a way of turning away from earthly tasks and sorrows. He thought that the Old Testament, with its concern for land, family, justice and the blessing of ordinary life, was a needed corrective. The Christian hope of resurrection, he wrote in effect, does not lift a person out of the world, but sends him back into it in a new way — to love, to work, to suffer and to serve, as Christ did.

This was not a denial of the life to come. It was a warning against using that life as an escape hatch. The hope that leaves the world to its fate is not the hope of the gospel. The hope that comes from the risen Christ gives courage to take on the tasks of this world, because we know they are not the end.

For I know the thoughts that I think toward you, saith the LORD, thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you an expected end. JEREMIAH 29:11

He lived that way himself. In the middle of the war, with his own future uncertain, he became engaged to be married. It was an act of hope in the goodness of ordinary life, made in the teeth of the times. It recalls the prophet Jeremiah, who, while Jerusalem was under siege, bought a field, because God had promised that fields and vineyards would one day be bought again in that land.

For thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel; Houses and fields and vineyards shall be possessed again in this land. JEREMIAH 32:15

Sheltered by good powers

In December 1944, in the Gestapo prison in Berlin, Bonhoeffer wrote a poem and sent it as a New Year’s greeting to those he loved. It has since been set to music and is sung in German churches to this day. Its theme is simple: that he and they were held, even then, by the kindness of God — surrounded and sheltered by good powers they could not see — and that whatever the coming year held, even if it held suffering, could be received from the hand of a Father who is good.

These are not the words of a man who expected rescue. By then he knew his situation was grave. They are the words of a man who had learned to trust God in the dark.

He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty. I will say of the LORD, He is my refuge and my fortress: my God; in him will I trust. PSALM 91:1–2

Death as freedom

Another prison poem traces what he called the stations on the road to freedom: discipline, action, suffering and, last of all, death. He pictured death not as the enemy that has the final word, but as the last stage of the journey, the moment when a believer is at last set free to see God. He did not speak of death lightly. He loved life, and he was young. But he had learned to see the grave as a door rather than a wall.

For I am in a strait betwixt two, having a desire to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better. PHILIPPIANS 1:23

The last Sunday

On Sunday 8 April 1945, in the schoolhouse at Schönberg where a group of prisoners was being held, Bonhoeffer was asked to lead a short service. He did so, reading and speaking on two texts. One was from the prophecy of the suffering servant.

But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed. ISAIAH 53:5

The other was from the first letter of Peter.

Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, which according to his abundant mercy hath begotten us again unto a lively hope by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead. 1 PETER 1:3

The cross and the resurrection: the whole of his theology, in two verses, preached to fellow prisoners on the last full day of his life. Soon after, two men came to take him away.

According to the recollection of Captain Payne Best, a British prisoner who was with him, Bonhoeffer asked Best to pass on a message to his friend Bishop George Bell in England — the substance of which was that this was the end, but for him the beginning of life. Best wrote this down some years later, and it is right to treat it as his memory of the words rather than an exact record. But it fits everything Bonhoeffer had written. He was hanged at Flossenbürg early the next morning.

A lively hope

What does his hope teach us? First, that Christian hope is not wishful thinking. It rests on a fact: the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead. Bonhoeffer did not hope in human progress, or in his own survival, or even in the defeat of the regime. He hoped in the God who raises the dead.

But is now made manifest by the appearing of our Saviour Jesus Christ, who hath abolished death, and hath brought life and immortality to light through the gospel. 2 TIMOTHY 1:10

Second, that Christian hope does not make us careless of this world. It makes us brave in it. Bonhoeffer went back to Germany, served, resisted, loved, got engaged, wrote letters of comfort, led a service for frightened men — all because he believed that death was not the last word.

Third, that Christian hope can be held in weakness. Bonhoeffer was afraid at times. He did not always know who he was. He did not know whether he would live. But he knew whose he was, and he trusted that nothing could separate him from God’s love.

For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, Nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord. ROMANS 8:38–39

That is the hope into which every Christian is born again. For Bonhoeffer the end came early and violently. For most of us it will come more quietly. But for all who are in Christ, the end is the beginning of life.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Ask whether your hope of heaven makes you braver in this world or more careless of it. Take one step of faithful action in the world this week because of your hope.

2. Do one act of hope in dark times — plant something, plan something, commit to something — as a sign that God’s future is good.

3. Read Romans 8:31–39 aloud and name, one by one, the things you fear might separate you from God’s love.

4. Think about your own death. Write a short prayer committing it into God’s hands, and keep it.

5. Read 1 Peter 1:3–9 each morning this week, and give thanks for the living hope of the resurrection.

A PRAYER
Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has begotten us again to a living hope by the resurrection of Jesus from the dead.
Lord, keep me from a hope that runs away from the world. Give me a hope that sends me back into it, to love and serve and suffer, as You did.
Shelter me with Your good powers in every dark hour. Let me receive from Your hand whatever You give, trusting that it comes from love.
And when my own end comes, let it be for me, as it was for Your servant, the beginning of life, through Jesus Christ, who was wounded for my sins and raised for my hope. Amen.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
Jesus saith unto him, If I will that he tarry till I come, what is that to thee? follow thou me. JOHN 21:22

We have covered a good deal of ground in sixteen short chapters — from costly grace to the Psalms, from the seminary at Finkenwalde to the cell at Tegel, from the Sermon on the Mount to the gallows at Flossenbürg. It would be easy to close the book with the impression that Bonhoeffer taught many different things. In truth he asked one question, over and over, in every setting of his short life: who is Jesus Christ, and what does it mean to follow him here and now?

One question, many answers

Costly grace is that question asked of the comfortable church. The Sermon on the Mount asks it of our daily conduct; Life Together asks it of our congregations and our ordinary days; the prison letters ask it in the darkest hours of a nation’s history. And the beginning of life is the question answered in the face of death.

At every point the answer came back to a person. Not a programme, not an ideal, not even a doctrine, but Jesus Christ, who is present and who calls.

Carrying it home

The peculiar danger of reading about Bonhoeffer is that we may admire him instead of following his Lord. His life makes a compelling story, and his phrases are memorable. It is possible to know all about cheap and costly grace and never pay anything. It is possible to quote Life Together and still despise one’s own congregation. Bonhoeffer would have seen that danger at once. He thought a knowledge of Christ that does not issue in obedience is not knowledge at all.

Therefore whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock. MATTHEW 7:24

So the plainest counsel this book can give is this. Go back to the chapter that troubled you most. Take its application points and do them, one at a time. Then go on to the next. Expect it to be ordinary. Most of discipleship is not martyrdom but faithfulness in small things — a word held back, an ear lent, a psalm prayed, a sin confessed, a neighbour served.

An honest word about the man

We have tried in these pages to be honest about Bonhoeffer. His part in the conspiracy against Hitler remains a matter on which faithful Christians disagree. His prison fragments were unfinished, and have been pulled in directions he would not have recognised. His Lutheran and academic background led him to positions many readers will not share. His life has been retold with more heroism than the record allows, and sayings have been put into his mouth that he never said.

None of this has been raised in order to diminish him. It has been raised because he would have insisted on it. The man who warned against cheap grace would not have wanted cheap praise. He did not want disciples of his own. He wanted people to follow Jesus Christ.

Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God. HEBREWS 12:2

Follow thou me

At the end of John’s Gospel, Peter, just restored after his denial, looks at another disciple and asks what will become of him. Jesus answers that it is none of Peter’s business. Follow thou me. That word is for us too, at the end of a book about another disciple. What became of Bonhoeffer is a matter for gratitude and for sober reflection. But the question that matters for the reader is not what he did. It is what we shall do, when the same Lord calls us, in our own time and place, to follow him.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Look back at the sentence you wrote at the start of this book about what it costs to be a Christian. Would you write it differently now?

2. Choose the chapter that troubled you most. Take its application points and act on one of them this week.

3. Choose one of Bonhoeffer’s own books from the guide that follows, and read it slowly, with the Bible open.

4. Share one thing you have learned with another believer, and ask them to hold you to it.

5. Ask the Lord plainly what following Him will mean for you in the coming year, and write down what He shows you.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus Christ, You called Your servant, and he followed You to the end. You call me too.
Forgive me for being more interested in other disciples than in following You myself. Let me not admire where I should obey.
Take what I have read and press it into my life until it costs me something. Begin with the chapter I would rather forget.
Keep my eyes on You, the author and finisher of my faith. Whatever the road, let me hear Your voice and follow You. Amen.

fields.title: A Reader’s Guide to Dietrich Bonhoeffer
fields.body_html:
Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me. JOHN 5:39

Bonhoeffer’s writings, and their English translations, are in copyright, and none of them is in the Ochorus library. They are widely available from their publishers. The standard scholarly edition in English is the Dietrich Bonhoeffer Works, published by Fortress Press in seventeen volumes, with careful introductions and notes; older translations of the best-known books remain in print and are perfectly usable for ordinary reading. What follows is a guide arranged for usefulness rather than chronology.

Begin here

Life Together (1939). The best place to start. Short, practical and searching, written out of the common life at Finkenwalde. Read it slowly, a chapter at a time, and let it examine your own congregation and your own heart.

Discipleship (1937), long known in English as The Cost of Discipleship. His most famous book. Read the opening chapters on costly grace and the call to follow, then the exposition of the Sermon on the Mount. The second part, on the church, is less read and worth the effort.

Psalms: The Prayer Book of the Bible (1940). A very short book, and a fine introduction to praying the Psalms.

The prison years

Letters and Papers from Prison, edited by Eberhard Bethge. Letters, poems and fragments from Tegel and after, first published in the 1950s. Moving and unsettling. Read it whole rather than in quotations, and read the letters about religionless Christianity alongside those about prayer and the secret discipline.

The letters he exchanged with Maria von Wedemeyer, published in English in the 1990s as Love Letters from Cell 92, show a more personal side of him.

For deeper study

Ethics. The unfinished book he regarded as his main work, gathered from fragments after his death. Demanding, and essential for understanding his thinking on responsibility and on the conspiracy.

Sanctorum Communio. His doctoral dissertation on the church. Difficult, but the source of his teaching that the church is Christ existing as community.

Creation and Fall. Lectures on the opening chapters of Genesis, given in Berlin in 1932–33. Fresh and theological rather than technical.

Christ the Center, also published as Christology. His 1933 lectures on the person of Christ, reconstructed from students’ notes. Short and dense.

Approach with care

The prison fragments on a world come of age and a religionless Christianity were unfinished thoughts. They have been quoted in support of positions — including a Christianity without a personal God — that his life and other writings contradict. Read them in the context of the whole man.

Be careful also with quotations attributed to him online and in popular books. Several of the best known are not his.

About Bonhoeffer

Eberhard Bethge, Dietrich Bonhoeffer: Theologian, Christian, Contemporary. The standard biography, by his closest friend and the editor of his letters. Long, detailed and indispensable.

Ferdinand Schlingensiepen, Dietrich Bonhoeffer 1906–1945: Martyr, Thinker, Man of Resistance. A shorter, reliable modern life.

Charles Marsh, Strange Glory: A Life of Dietrich Bonhoeffer (2014). A well-researched and humane biography, attentive to his inner life.

Eric Metaxas, Bonhoeffer: Pastor, Martyr, Prophet, Spy (2010). Popular and widely read, especially among evangelicals. Many scholars have criticised it for presenting him in terms closer to modern evangelicalism than the record allows; read it, if at all, alongside one of the others.

Reggie L. Williams, Bonhoeffer’s Black Jesus (2014). On the influence of the Harlem church on his life and thought.

Reading more than one of these is wise. Bonhoeffer has been claimed by many camps, and no single account is disinterested.

Three counsels for reading him

Read him with the Bible open. He would have insisted on it. His own authority was always Scripture, and his books are meant to send you back to it.

Read him whole. Do not take only the Bonhoeffer your tradition prefers — the evangelical of Discipleship or the radical of the prison letters. They are the same man.

Read him to obey. He had little patience with knowledge that never became action. A page read and acted upon is worth more than a volume admired.

Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord. COLOSSIANS 3:16
